title: Career Fair: UI/UX Design
description:
We want to be upfront about what this event is not. It is not a placement coaching session. It is not a certificate farm. It is not a box to tick on your co-curricular activity sheet. It is a room full of people who are genuinely curious about UI/UX Design, facilitated by people who have invested real time in understanding it, with the goal of leaving everyone slightly less confused than they arrived. If that sounds like a good way to spend a few hours, the door is open.

Here is what the session actually looks like. We open with a fifteen-minute orientation that covers the landscape of UI/UX Design — where it sits relative to everything else you have learned, why it matters now more than it did five years ago, and what a working professional actually does with it on a Monday morning. This part is deliberately fast. We do not want to spend half the session on theory that you could have absorbed from a Wikipedia article. We want to get to the part where you do things.

Most events on UI/UX Design are designed for people who already have a foundation and just want to go deeper. This one is different. Eco Warriors built this session specifically for the student who has heard the term a hundred times, nodded along in class, and quietly panicked when asked to actually do something with it. You are the target audience. There is no shame in being here at the beginning — there is only the question of what you choose to do about it. This is your practical starting point.

This is Eco Warriors's commitment: if you attend and feel it was not worth your time, tell us directly. We will listen and we will fix it for next time. That is how we have gotten better every semester.

title: Hands-on Competitive Programming Session
description:
There is a version of this event that would have been easy to run — a polished slide deck, a speaker talking at you for ninety minutes, a group photo at the end. We chose not to do that version. Instead, the Cultural Committee spent the last month building a session on Competitive Programming that puts you in the driver's seat from the first minute. The facilitators are here as guides, not lecturers. The agenda is a suggestion, not a script. And the only metric we care about at the end is whether you leave more capable than when you arrived.

A few things we want to be transparent about. The facilitators running this session are not perfect. They will make mistakes in live demonstrations. When that happens, we will debug together, which is arguably the most educational part of any session. Cultural Committee believes in showing real work, not curated performances. If that sounds like a good use of your Saturday afternoon, we think you will find this event genuinely worthwhile.

The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from Competitive Programming that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

The person leading today's session on Competitive Programming was not our first choice — they were our third. Our first two choices were excellent but unavailable on this date. Our third choice turned out to be better than either of the first two, which is a useful reminder that the best facilitators are not always the most obvious ones. They bring a perspective on Competitive Programming that we had not fully anticipated when we reached out, and we think it makes the session richer for it.

Food and drinks will be available throughout. We mention this not to bribe you into attending — the content should do that — but because we have noticed that sessions run better when people are not hungry. Please eat something before you arrive as well. A three-hour session on Competitive Programming on an empty stomach is not the optimal learning environment, and we speak from experience.

Seats will run out before the deadline does. Register now.

title: Panel Discussion: System Design
description:
A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with System Design professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. But if you are hoping for a deep technical dive at the cutting edge of the field, this is not that event. We are going for breadth and confidence-building, not depth. The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

Welcome to one of the most genuinely useful events Cultural Committee has run this academic year. We know that phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let us be specific about what we mean. This session on System Design was designed in response to direct feedback from students who sat placement interviews, bombed questions they had never been exposed to, and came back asking us to do something about it. We listened. What you will see today is the result of six weeks of curriculum design, two rounds of feedback from working engineers, and one very honest conversation about what actually matters.

The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for System Design — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

We considered bringing in an external speaker for this one and decided against it. The best person to talk to RVCE students about navigating System Design in the current environment is someone who was an RVCE student recently enough to remember what it felt like — and senior enough to have perspective on it. That is what we have. Someone who has been where you are, done what you are trying to do, and is willing to be honest about how they actually got there.

After the event, all registered attendees will receive a curated resource pack: three links our facilitators actually use, two books they would recommend if pressed, and one honest assessment of the gaps in their own knowledge of System Design and how they are addressing them. We include the last one because we think intellectual honesty about what you do not know is as valuable as knowledge itself, and we want to model that for students.

Show up. Work hard. Leave better. That is all we ask.

title: Machine Learning Hackathon
description:
One thing that consistently surprises attendees at Open Source Club events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on Machine Learning — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. They are a core part of what we are trying to create.

We have structured this event around a principle that Open Source Club cares about deeply: learning by producing, not learning by consuming. Every segment of this session on Machine Learning includes a moment where you must make something — a diagram, a line of code, a decision, a prediction. These are not graded. They will not be collected. They are for you, because the act of producing forces your brain to process information in a way that passive watching simply does not.

There is a version of this event that would have been easy to run — a polished slide deck, a speaker talking at you for ninety minutes, a group photo at the end. We chose not to do that version. Instead, the Open Source Club spent the last month building a session on Machine Learning that puts you in the driver's seat from the first minute. The facilitators are here as guides, not lecturers. The agenda is a suggestion, not a script. And the only metric we care about at the end is whether you leave more capable than when you arrived.

The speakers for this event have been chosen for one reason above all others: they can explain things clearly. It sounds obvious, but it is surprisingly rare. We have had sessions in the past where technically brilliant people presented information in a way that left the room more confused than when they arrived. We learnt from that. The facilitators you will hear from today have been tested in smaller settings first, given feedback, and iterated. What you are getting is a refined version, not a first draft.

The venue has been chosen specifically for its layout. We needed a room where the facilitator could move around freely, where breakout discussions could happen without disrupting the main session, and where the acoustics would not turn every explanation into an echo. We did a walkthrough last week. The space works. If you have attended events at other venues and found them frustrating for these reasons, this one should be different.

We will see you there. Bring your laptop, bring your questions, and bring someone who needs this as much as you do.

title: Career Fair: Machine Learning
description:
We want to be upfront about what this event is not. It is not a placement coaching session. It is not a certificate farm. It is not a box to tick on your co-curricular activity sheet. It is a room full of people who are genuinely curious about Machine Learning, facilitated by people who have invested real time in understanding it, with the goal of leaving everyone slightly less confused than they arrived. If that sounds like a good way to spend a few hours, the door is open.

The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from Machine Learning that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

The idea for this event on Machine Learning came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

If you have read this far and you are still not registered, we genuinely want to know what is stopping you. DM us on Instagram.

title: Annual AR/VR Development Competition
description:
There is a version of this event that would have been easy to run — a polished slide deck, a speaker talking at you for ninety minutes, a group photo at the end. We chose not to do that version. Instead, the Literary Club spent the last month building a session on AR/VR Development that puts you in the driver's seat from the first minute. The facilitators are here as guides, not lecturers. The agenda is a suggestion, not a script. And the only metric we care about at the end is whether you leave more capable than when you arrived.

A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with AR/VR Development professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. But if you are hoping for a deep technical dive at the cutting edge of the field, this is not that event. We are going for breadth and confidence-building, not depth. The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

We have structured this event around a principle that Literary Club cares about deeply: learning by producing, not learning by consuming. Every segment of this session on AR/VR Development includes a moment where you must make something — a diagram, a line of code, a decision, a prediction. These are not graded. They will not be collected. They are for you, because the act of producing forces your brain to process information in a way that passive watching simply does not.

The speakers for this event have been chosen for one reason above all others: they can explain things clearly. It sounds obvious, but it is surprisingly rare. We have had sessions in the past where technically brilliant people presented information in a way that left the room more confused than when they arrived. We learnt from that. The facilitators you will hear from today have been tested in smaller settings first, given feedback, and iterated. What you are getting is a refined version, not a first draft.

Certificates of participation will be issued to everyone who attends. We know that is a secondary concern for most people in this room, and we are glad for that. But for those who need it — for internship applications, for placement interviews, for anxious parents — it exists and it will arrive in your inbox within 48 hours of the event's close. Please register with your college email address to ensure delivery.

This is Literary Club's commitment: if you attend and feel it was not worth your time, tell us directly. We will listen and we will fix it for next time. That is how we have gotten better every semester.

title: Industry Talk: React & Next.js
description:
The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for React & Next.js — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

We want to be upfront about what this event is not. It is not a placement coaching session. It is not a certificate farm. It is not a box to tick on your co-curricular activity sheet. It is a room full of people who are genuinely curious about React & Next.js, facilitated by people who have invested real time in understanding it, with the goal of leaving everyone slightly less confused than they arrived. If that sounds like a good way to spend a few hours, the door is open.

Welcome to one of the most genuinely useful events IEEE Student Branch has run this academic year. We know that phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let us be specific about what we mean. This session on React & Next.js was designed in response to direct feedback from students who sat placement interviews, bombed questions they had never been exposed to, and came back asking us to do something about it. We listened. What you will see today is the result of six weeks of curriculum design, two rounds of feedback from working engineers, and one very honest conversation about what actually matters.

Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where React & Next.js was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with React & Next.js. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together.

Registration is open now. Space is limited. If you are on the fence, the fence is the wrong place to be.

title: Entrepreneurship — Guest Lecture
description:
We want to be upfront about what this event is not. It is not a placement coaching session. It is not a certificate farm. It is not a box to tick on your co-curricular activity sheet. It is a room full of people who are genuinely curious about Entrepreneurship, facilitated by people who have invested real time in understanding it, with the goal of leaving everyone slightly less confused than they arrived. If that sounds like a good way to spend a few hours, the door is open.

There is a version of this event that would have been easy to run — a polished slide deck, a speaker talking at you for ninety minutes, a group photo at the end. We chose not to do that version. Instead, the Debate Society spent the last month building a session on Entrepreneurship that puts you in the driver's seat from the first minute. The facilitators are here as guides, not lecturers. The agenda is a suggestion, not a script. And the only metric we care about at the end is whether you leave more capable than when you arrived.

The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for Entrepreneurship — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

The person leading today's session on Entrepreneurship was not our first choice — they were our third. Our first two choices were excellent but unavailable on this date. Our third choice turned out to be better than either of the first two, which is a useful reminder that the best facilitators are not always the most obvious ones. They bring a perspective on Entrepreneurship that we had not fully anticipated when we reached out, and we think it makes the session richer for it.

If you have read this far and you are still not registered, we genuinely want to know what is stopping you. DM us on Instagram.

title: Web Dev Workshop: DevOps
description: Welcome to one of the most genuinely useful events Literary Club has run this academic year. We know that phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let us be specific about what we mean. This session on DevOps was designed in response to direct feedback from students who sat placement interviews, bombed questions they had never been exposed to, and came back asking us to do something about it. We listened. What you will see today is the result of six weeks of curriculum design, two rounds of feedback from working engineers, and one very honest conversation about what actually matters. We want to be upfront about what this event is not. It is not a placement coaching session. It is not a certificate farm. It is not a box to tick on your co-curricular activity sheet. It is a room full of people who are genuinely curious about DevOps, facilitated by people who have invested real time in understanding it, with the goal of leaving everyone slightly less confused than they arrived. If that sounds like a good way to spend a few hours, the door is open. The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from DevOps that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday. Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where DevOps was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with DevOps. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together. Registration is open now. Space is limited. If you are on the fence, the fence is the wrong place to be. Registration open now & closing soon. <Limited seats> available — don't miss out.

In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

We considered bringing in an external speaker for this one and decided against it. The best person to talk to RVCE students about navigating DevOps in the current environment is someone who was an RVCE student recently enough to remember what it felt like — and senior enough to have perspective on it. description:

Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where Cybersecurity was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with Cybersecurity. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together.

title: Cybersecurity — Guest Lecture
description:
There is a version of this event that would have been easy to run — a polished slide deck, a speaker talking at you for ninety minutes, a group photo at the end. We chose not to do that version. Instead, the Robotics Club spent the last month building a session on Cybersecurity that puts you in the driver's seat from the first minute. The facilitators are here as guides, not lecturers. The agenda is a suggestion, not a script. And the only metric we care about at the end is whether you leave more capable than when you arrived.

One thing that consistently surprises attendees at Robotics Club events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on Cybersecurity — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. They are a core part of what we are trying to create.

The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from Cybersecurity that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where Cybersecurity was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with Cybersecurity. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together.

We will see you there. Bring your laptop, bring your questions, and bring someone who needs this as much as you do.

title: System Design — Guest Lecture
description:

It is a room full of people who are genuinely curious about System Design, facilitated by people who have invested real time in understanding it, with the goal of leaving everyone slightly less confused than they arrived. If that sounds like a good way to spend a few hours, the door is open.

The idea for this event on System Design came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

We have structured this event around a principle that Entrepreneurship Cell cares about deeply: learning by producing, not learning by consuming. Every segment of this session on System Design includes a moment where you must make something — a diagram, a line of code, a decision, a prediction. These are not graded. They will not be collected. They are for you, because the act of producing forces your brain to process information in a way that passive watching simply does not.

The speakers for this event have been chosen for one reason above all others: they can explain things clearly. It sounds obvious, but it is surprisingly rare. We have had sessions in the past where technically brilliant people presented information in a way that left the room more confused than when they arrived. We learnt from that. The facilitators you will hear from today have been tested in smaller settings first, given feedback, and iterated. What you are getting is a refined version, not a first draft.

If you have read this far and you are still not registered, we genuinely want to know what is stopping you. DM us on Instagram.

title: Career Fair: Career Prep & Placement
description:

The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from Career Prep & Placement that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

The idea for this event on Career Prep & Placement came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where Career Prep & Placement was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with Career Prep & Placement. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together.

After the event, all registered attendees will receive a curated resource pack: three links our facilitators actually use, two books they would recommend if pressed, and one honest assessment of the gaps in their own knowledge of Career Prep & Placement and how they are addressing them. We will see you there. Bring your laptop, bring your questions, and bring someone who needs this as much as you do.

title: Industry Talk: Research Methodology
description:
Welcome to one of the most genuinely useful events Quizzing Club has run this academic year. We know that phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let us be specific about what we mean. This session on Research Methodology was designed in response to direct feedback from students who sat placement interviews, bombed questions they had never been exposed to, and came back asking us to do something about it. We listened. What you will see today is the result of six weeks of curriculum design, two rounds of feedback from working engineers, and one very honest conversation about what actually matters.

We want to be upfront about what this event is not. It is not a placement coaching session. It is not a certificate farm. It is not a box to tick on your co-curricular activity sheet. It is a room full of people who are genuinely curious about Research Methodology, facilitated by people who have invested real time in understanding it, with the goal of leaving everyone slightly less confused than they arrived. If that sounds like a good way to spend a few hours, the door is open.

Here is what the session actually looks like. We open with a fifteen-minute orientation that covers the landscape of Research Methodology — where it sits relative to everything else you have learned, why it matters now more than it did five years ago, and what a working professional actually does with it on a Monday morning. This part is deliberately fast. We do not want to spend half the session on theory that you could have absorbed from a Wikipedia article. We want to get to the part where you do things.

After the event, all registered attendees will receive a curated resource pack: three links our facilitators actually use, two books they would recommend if pressed, and one honest assessment of the gaps in their own knowledge of Research Methodology and how they are addressing them. We include the last one because we think intellectual honesty about what you do not know is as valuable as knowledge itself, and we want to model that for students.

We will see you there. Bring your laptop, bring your questions, and bring someone who needs this as much as you do.

title: Open Mic: UI/UX Design
description:
The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for UI/UX Design — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

The idea for this event on UI/UX Design came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

When that happens, we will debug together, which is arguably the most educational part of any session. Finance Club believes in showing real work, not curated performances. If that sounds like a good use of your Saturday afternoon, we think you will find this event genuinely worthwhile.

The person leading today's session on UI/UX Design was not our first choice — they were our third. Our first two choices were excellent but unavailable on this date. Our third choice turned out to be better than either of the first two, which is a useful reminder that the best facilitators are not always the most obvious ones. They bring a perspective on UI/UX Design that we had not fully anticipated when we reached out, and we think it makes the session richer for it.

The venue has been chosen specifically for its layout. We needed a room where the facilitator could move around freely, where breakout discussions could happen without disrupting the main session, and where the acoustics would not turn every explanation into an echo. title: Python for Beginners Showcase
description:
A few things we want to be transparent about. The facilitators running this session are not perfect. They will make mistakes in live demonstrations. When that happens, we will debug together, which is arguably the most educational part of any session. Open Source Club believes in showing real work, not curated performances. If that sounds like a good use of your Saturday afternoon, we think you will find this event genuinely worthwhile.

Welcome to one of the most genuinely useful events Open Source Club has run this academic year. We know that phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let us be specific about what we mean. This session on Python for Beginners was designed in response to direct feedback from students who sat placement interviews, bombed questions they had never been exposed to, and came back asking us to do something about it. We listened. What you will see today is the result of six weeks of curriculum design, two rounds of feedback from working engineers, and one very honest conversation about what actually matters.

Here is what the session actually looks like. We open with a fifteen-minute orientation that covers the landscape of Python for Beginners — where it sits relative to everything else you have learned, why it matters now more than it did five years ago, and what a working professional actually does with it on a Monday morning. This part is deliberately fast. We do not want to spend half the session on theory that you could have absorbed from a Wikipedia article. We want to get to the part where you do things.

The person leading today's session on Python for Beginners was not our first choice — they were our third. Our first two choices were excellent but unavailable on this date. Our third choice turned out to be better than either of the first two, which is a useful reminder that the best facilitators are not always the most obvious ones. They bring a perspective on Python for Beginners that we had not fully anticipated when we reached out, and we think it makes the session richer for it.

After the event, all registered attendees will receive a curated resource pack: three links our facilitators actually use, two books they would recommend if pressed, and one honest assessment of the gaps in their own knowledge of Python for Beginners and how they are addressing them. We include the last one because we think intellectual honesty about what you do not know is as valuable as knowledge itself, and we want to model that for students.

Registration is open now. Space is limited. If you are on the fence, the fence is the wrong place to be.

description:

One thing that consistently surprises attendees at Eco Warriors events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. Food and drinks will be available throughout. title: Seminar on Finance 101
description:
A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with Finance 101 professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. title: Annual DevOps Competition
description:
The idea for this event on DevOps came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from DevOps that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with DevOps professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. But if you are hoping for a deep technical dive at the cutting edge of the field, this is not that event. We are going for breadth and confidence-building, not depth. The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

The person leading today's session on DevOps was not our first choice — they were our third. Our first two choices were excellent but unavailable on this date. Our third choice turned out to be better than either of the first two, which is a useful reminder that the best facilitators are not always the most obvious ones. They bring a perspective on DevOps that we had not fully anticipated when we reached out, and we think it makes the session richer for it.

After the event, all registered attendees will receive a curated resource pack: three links our facilitators actually use, two books they would recommend if pressed, and one honest assessment of the gaps in their own knowledge of DevOps and how they are addressing them. We include the last one because we think intellectual honesty about what you do not know is as valuable as knowledge itself, and we want to model that for students.

We will see you there. Bring your laptop, bring your questions, and bring someone who needs this as much as you do.

title: Career Fair: DevOps
description:
There is a version of this event that would have been easy to run — a polished slide deck, a speaker talking at you for ninety minutes, a group photo at the end. We chose not to do that version. Instead, the Sports Council spent the last month building a session on DevOps that puts you in the driver's seat from the first minute. The facilitators are here as guides, not lecturers. The agenda is a suggestion, not a script. And the only metric we care about at the end is whether you leave more capable than when you arrived.

One thing that consistently surprises attendees at Sports Council events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on DevOps — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. They are a core part of what we are trying to create.

We have structured this event around a principle that Sports Council cares about deeply: learning by producing, not learning by consuming. Every segment of this session on DevOps includes a moment where you must make something — a diagram, a line of code, a decision, a prediction. These are not graded. They will not be collected. They are for you, because the act of producing forces your brain to process information in a way that passive watching simply does not.

The speakers for this event have been chosen for one reason above all others: they can explain things clearly. It sounds obvious, but it is surprisingly rare. We have had sessions in the past where technically brilliant people presented information in a way that left the room more confused than when they arrived. We learnt from that. The facilitators you will hear from today have been tested in smaller settings first, given feedback, and iterated. What you are getting is a refined version, not a first draft.

After the event, all registered attendees will receive a curated resource pack: three links our facilitators actually use, two books they would recommend if pressed, and one honest assessment of the gaps in their own knowledge of DevOps and how they are addressing them. We include the last one because we think intellectual honesty about what you do not know is as valuable as knowledge itself, and we want to model that for students.

Show up. Work hard. Leave better. That is all we ask.

title: Industry Talk: Machine Learning
description:
Here is what the session actually looks like. We open with a fifteen-minute orientation that covers the landscape of Machine Learning — where it sits relative to everything else you have learned, why it matters now more than it did five years ago, and what a working professional actually does with it on a Monday morning. This part is deliberately fast. We do not want to spend half the session on theory that you could have absorbed from a Wikipedia article. We want to get to the part where you do things.

There is a version of this event that would have been easy to run — a polished slide deck, a speaker talking at you for ninety minutes, a group photo at the end. We chose not to do that version. Instead, the Cybersecurity Club spent the last month building a session on Machine Learning that puts you in the driver's seat from the first minute. The facilitators are here as guides, not lecturers. The agenda is a suggestion, not a script. And the only metric we care about at the end is whether you leave more capable than when you arrived.

A few things we want to be transparent about. The facilitators running this session are not perfect. They will make mistakes in live demonstrations. When that happens, we will debug together, which is arguably the most educational part of any session. Cybersecurity Club believes in showing real work, not curated performances. If that sounds like a good use of your Saturday afternoon, we think you will find this event genuinely worthwhile.

The person leading today's session on Machine Learning was not our first choice — they were our third. Our first two choices were excellent but unavailable on this date. Our third choice turned out to be better than either of the first two, which is a useful reminder that the best facilitators are not always the most obvious ones. They bring a perspective on Machine Learning that we had not fully anticipated when we reached out, and we think it makes the session richer for it.

The venue has been chosen specifically for its layout. We needed a room where the facilitator could move around freely, where breakout discussions could happen without disrupting the main session, and where the acoustics would not turn every explanation into an echo. We did a walkthrough last week. The space works. If you have attended events at other venues and found them frustrating for these reasons, this one should be different.

We will see you there. Bring your laptop, bring your questions, and bring someone who needs this as much as you do.

title: Annual Cloud Computing Competition
description:
One thing that consistently surprises attendees at Cybersecurity Club events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on Cloud Computing — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. They are a core part of what we are trying to create.

We have structured this event around a principle that Cybersecurity Club cares about deeply: learning by producing, not learning by consuming. Every segment of this session on Cloud Computing includes a moment where you must make something — a diagram, a line of code, a decision, a prediction. These are not graded. They will not be collected. They are for you, because the act of producing forces your brain to process information in a way that passive watching simply does not.

The idea for this event on Cloud Computing came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

We considered bringing in an external speaker for this one and decided against it. The best person to talk to RVCE students about navigating Cloud Computing in the current environment is someone who was an RVCE student recently enough to remember what it felt like — and senior enough to have perspective on it. That is what we have. Someone who has been where you are, done what you are trying to do, and is willing to be honest about how they actually got there.

Certificates of participation will be issued to everyone who attends. We know that is a secondary concern for most people in this room, and we are glad for that. But for those who need it — for internship applications, for placement interviews, for anxious parents — it exists and it will arrive in your inbox within 48 hours of the event's close. Please register with your college email address to ensure delivery.

We will see you there. Bring your laptop, bring your questions, and bring someone who needs this as much as you do.

title: DevOps — Guest Lecture
description:
We want to be upfront about what this event is not. It is not a placement coaching session. It is not a certificate farm. It is not a box to tick on your co-curricular activity sheet. It is a room full of people who are genuinely curious about DevOps, facilitated by people who have invested real time in understanding it, with the goal of leaving everyone slightly less confused than they arrived. If that sounds like a good way to spend a few hours, the door is open.

The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for DevOps — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

Most events on DevOps are designed for people who already have a foundation and just want to go deeper. This one is different. Sports Council built this session specifically for the student who has heard the term a hundred times, nodded along in class, and quietly panicked when asked to actually do something with it. You are the target audience. There is no shame in being here at the beginning — there is only the question of what you choose to do about it. This is your practical starting point.

Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where DevOps was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with DevOps. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together.

We will see you there. Bring your laptop, bring your questions, and bring someone who needs this as much as you do.

title: Career Fair: Robotics & Automation
description:
The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from Robotics & Automation that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

The idea for this event on Robotics & Automation came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

One thing that consistently surprises attendees at Finance Club events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on Robotics & Automation — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. They are a core part of what we are trying to create.

The speakers for this event have been chosen for one reason above all others: they can explain things clearly. It sounds obvious, but it is surprisingly rare. We have had sessions in the past where technically brilliant people presented information in a way that left the room more confused than when they arrived. We learnt from that. The facilitators you will hear from today have been tested in smaller settings first, given feedback, and iterated. What you are getting is a refined version, not a first draft.

Registration is open now. Space is limited. If you are on the fence, the fence is the wrong place to be.

title: Open Mic: Cybersecurity
description:
Here is what the session actually looks like. We open with a fifteen-minute orientation that covers the landscape of Cybersecurity — where it sits relative to everything else you have learned, why it matters now more than it did five years ago, and what a working professional actually does with it on a Monday morning. This part is deliberately fast. We do not want to spend half the session on theory that you could have absorbed from a Wikipedia article. We want to get to the part where you do things.

A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with Cybersecurity professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. But if you are hoping for a deep technical dive at the cutting edge of the field, this is not that event. We are going for breadth and confidence-building, not depth. The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

There is a version of this event that would have been easy to run — a polished slide deck, a speaker talking at you for ninety minutes, a group photo at the end. We chose not to do that version. Instead, the Debate Society spent the last month building a session on Cybersecurity that puts you in the driver's seat from the first minute. The facilitators are here as guides, not lecturers. The agenda is a suggestion, not a script. And the only metric we care about at the end is whether you leave more capable than when you arrived.

We considered bringing in an external speaker for this one and decided against it. The best person to talk to RVCE students about navigating Cybersecurity in the current environment is someone who was an RVCE student recently enough to remember what it felt like — and senior enough to have perspective on it. That is what we have. Someone who has been where you are, done what you are trying to do, and is willing to be honest about how they actually got there.

Seats will run out before the deadline does. Register now.

title: Photography Basics Sprint
description:
The idea for this event on Photography Basics came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with Photography Basics professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. But if you are hoping for a deep technical dive at the cutting edge of the field, this is not that event. We are going for breadth and confidence-building, not depth. The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

We have structured this event around a principle that Music Society cares about deeply: learning by producing, not learning by consuming. Every segment of this session on Photography Basics includes a moment where you must make something — a diagram, a line of code, a decision, a prediction. These are not graded. They will not be collected. They are for you, because the act of producing forces your brain to process information in a way that passive watching simply does not.

Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where Photography Basics was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with Photography Basics. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together.

After the event, all registered attendees will receive a curated resource pack: three links our facilitators actually use, two books they would recommend if pressed, and one honest assessment of the gaps in their own knowledge of Photography Basics and how they are addressing them. We include the last one because we think intellectual honesty about what you do not know is as valuable as knowledge itself, and we want to model that for students.

This is Music Society's commitment: if you attend and feel it was not worth your time, tell us directly. We will listen and we will fix it for next time. That is how we have gotten better every semester.

The idea for this event on Cybersecurity came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

We want to be upfront about what this event is not. It is not a placement coaching session. It is not a certificate farm. It is not a box to tick on your co-curricular activity sheet. It is a room full of people who are genuinely curious about Cybersecurity, facilitated by people who have invested real time in understanding it, with the goal of leaving everyone slightly less confused than they arrived. If that sounds like a good way to spend a few hours, the door is open.

The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for Cybersecurity — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where Cybersecurity was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with Cybersecurity. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together.

After the event, all registered attendees will receive a curated resource pack: three links our facilitators actually use, two books they would recommend if pressed, and one honest assessment of the gaps in their own knowledge of Cybersecurity and how they are addressing them. We include the last one because we think intellectual honesty about what you do not know is as valuable as knowledge itself, and we want to model that for students.

We will see you there. Bring your laptop, bring your questions, and bring someone who needs this as much as you do.

title: Finance 101 Sprint
description:
Most events on Finance 101 are designed for people who already have a foundation and just want to go deeper. This one is different. Photography Club built this session specifically for the student who has heard the term a hundred times, nodded along in class, and quietly panicked when asked to actually do something with it. You are the target audience. There is no shame in being here at the beginning — there is only the question of what you choose to do about it. This is your practical starting point.

We want to be upfront about what this event is not. It is not a placement coaching session. It is not a certificate farm. It is not a box to tick on your co-curricular activity sheet. It is a room full of people who are genuinely curious about Finance 101, facilitated by people who have invested real time in understanding it, with the goal of leaving everyone slightly less confused than they arrived. If that sounds like a good way to spend a few hours, the door is open.

The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from Finance 101 that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

We considered bringing in an external speaker for this one and decided against it. The best person to talk to RVCE students about navigating Finance 101 in the current environment is someone who was an RVCE student recently enough to remember what it felt like — and senior enough to have perspective on it. That is what we have. Someone who has been where you are, done what you are trying to do, and is willing to be honest about how they actually got there.

Certificates of participation will be issued to everyone who attends. We know that is a secondary concern for most people in this room, and we are glad for that. But for those who need it — for internship applications, for placement interviews, for anxious parents — it exists and it will arrive in your inbox within 48 hours of the event's close. Please register with your college email address to ensure delivery.

Registration is open now. Space is limited. If you are on the fence, the fence is the wrong place to be.

title: Hands-on DevOps Session
description:
Welcome to one of the most genuinely useful events Entrepreneurship Cell has run this academic year. We know that phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let us be specific about what we mean. The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together.

title: Blockchain Bootcamp
description:
Most events on Blockchain are designed for people who already have a foundation and just want to go deeper. This one is different. Coding Club RVCE built this session specifically for the student who has heard the term a hundred times, nodded along in class, and quietly panicked when asked to actually do something with it. You are the target audience. There is no shame in being here at the beginning — there is only the question of what you choose to do about it. This is your practical starting point.

We want to be upfront about what this event is not. It is not a placement coaching session. It is not a certificate farm. It is not a box to tick on your co-curricular activity sheet. It is a room full of people who are genuinely curious about Blockchain, facilitated by people who have invested real time in understanding it, with the goal of leaving everyone slightly less confused than they arrived. If that sounds like a good way to spend a few hours, the door is open.

The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from Blockchain that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

The speakers for this event have been chosen for one reason above all others: they can explain things clearly. It sounds obvious, but it is surprisingly rare. We have had sessions in the past where technically brilliant people presented information in a way that left the room more confused than when they arrived. We learnt from that. The facilitators you will hear from today have been tested in smaller settings first, given feedback, and iterated. What you are getting is a refined version, not a first draft.

If you have read this far and you are still not registered, we genuinely want to know what is stopping you. DM us on Instagram.

title: Hands-on Finance 101 Session
description:
The idea for this event on Finance 101 came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for Finance 101 — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

A few things we want to be transparent about. The facilitators running this session are not perfect. They will make mistakes in live demonstrations. When that happens, we will debug together, which is arguably the most educational part of any session. Finance Club believes in showing real work, not curated performances. If that sounds like a good use of your Saturday afternoon, we think you will find this event genuinely worthwhile.

The person leading today's session on Finance 101 was not our first choice — they were our third. Our first two choices were excellent but unavailable on this date. Our third choice turned out to be better than either of the first two, which is a useful reminder that the best facilitators are not always the most obvious ones. They bring a perspective on Finance 101 that we had not fully anticipated when we reached out, and we think it makes the session richer for it.

We will see you there. Bring your laptop, bring your questions, and bring someone who needs this as much as you do.

title: Game Development Sprint
description:
A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with Game Development professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. But if you are hoping for a deep technical dive at the cutting edge of the field, this is not that event. We are going for breadth and confidence-building, not depth. The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from Game Development that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

The idea for this event on Game Development came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where Game Development was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with Game Development. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together.

Registration is open now. Space is limited. If you are on the fence, the fence is the wrong place to be.

title: Open Source Contribution Hackathon
description:
A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with Open Source Contribution professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. But if you are hoping for a deep technical dive at the cutting edge of the field, this is not that event. We are going for breadth and confidence-building, not depth. The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for Open Source Contribution — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

Welcome to one of the most genuinely useful events Cybersecurity Club has run this academic year. We know that phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let us be specific about what we mean. This session on Open Source Contribution was designed in response to direct feedback from students who sat placement interviews, bombed questions they had never been exposed to, and came back asking us to do something about it. We listened. What you will see today is the result of six weeks of curriculum design, two rounds of feedback from working engineers, and one very honest conversation about what actually matters.

The person leading today's session on Open Source Contribution was not our first choice — they were our third. Our first two choices were excellent but unavailable on this date. Our third choice turned out to be better than either of the first two, which is a useful reminder that the best facilitators are not always the most obvious ones. They bring a perspective on Open Source Contribution that we had not fully anticipated when we reached out, and we think it makes the session richer for it.

We will see you there. Bring your laptop, bring your questions, and bring someone who needs this as much as you do.

title: Open Mic: Python for Beginners
description:
Welcome to one of the most genuinely useful events Cultural Committee has run this academic year. We know that phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let us be specific about what we mean. This session on Python for Beginners was designed in response to direct feedback from students who sat placement interviews, bombed questions they had never been exposed to, and came back asking us to do something about it. We listened. What you will see today is the result of six weeks of curriculum design, two rounds of feedback from working engineers, and one very honest conversation about what actually matters.

We have structured this event around a principle that Cultural Committee cares about deeply: learning by producing, not learning by consuming. Every segment of this session on Python for Beginners includes a moment where you must make something — a diagram, a line of code, a decision, a prediction. These are not graded. They will not be collected. They are for you, because the act of producing forces your brain to process information in a way that passive watching simply does not.

One thing that consistently surprises attendees at Cultural Committee events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on Python for Beginners — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. They are a core part of what we are trying to create.

We will see you there. Bring your laptop, bring your questions, and bring someone who needs this as much as you do.

title: Industry Talk: REST APIs
description:
There is a version of this event that would have been easy to run — a polished slide deck, a speaker talking at you for ninety minutes, a group photo at the end. We chose not to do that version. Instead, the Literary Club spent the last month building a session on REST APIs that puts you in the driver's seat from the first minute. The facilitators are here as guides, not lecturers. The agenda is a suggestion, not a script. And the only metric we care about at the end is whether you leave more capable than when you arrived.

Here is what the session actually looks like. We open with a fifteen-minute orientation that covers the landscape of REST APIs — where it sits relative to everything else you have learned, why it matters now more than it did five years ago, and what a working professional actually does with it on a Monday morning. This part is deliberately fast. We do not want to spend half the session on theory that you could have absorbed from a Wikipedia article. We want to get to the part where you do things.

We want to be upfront about what this event is not. It is not a placement coaching session. It is not a certificate farm. It is not a box to tick on your co-curricular activity sheet. It is a room full of people who are genuinely curious about REST APIs, facilitated by people who have invested real time in understanding it, with the goal of leaving everyone slightly less confused than they arrived. If that sounds like a good way to spend a few hours, the door is open.

The person leading today's session on REST APIs was not our first choice — they were our third. Our first two choices were excellent but unavailable on this date. Our third choice turned out to be better than either of the first two, which is a useful reminder that the best facilitators are not always the most obvious ones. They bring a perspective on REST APIs that we had not fully anticipated when we reached out, and we think it makes the session richer for it.

The venue has been chosen specifically for its layout. We needed a room where the facilitator could move around freely, where breakout discussions could happen without disrupting the main session, and where the acoustics would not turn every explanation into an echo. We did a walkthrough last week. The space works. If you have attended events at other venues and found them frustrating for these reasons, this one should be different.

Registration is open now. Space is limited. If you are on the fence, the fence is the wrong place to be.

title: Open Mic: Competitive Programming
description:
The idea for this event on Competitive Programming came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

We want to be upfront about what this event is not. It is not a placement coaching session. It is not a certificate farm. It is not a box to tick on your co-curricular activity sheet. It is a room full of people who are genuinely curious about Competitive Programming, facilitated by people who have invested real time in understanding it, with the goal of leaving everyone slightly less confused than they arrived. If that sounds like a good way to spend a few hours, the door is open.

The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for Competitive Programming — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

The speakers for this event have been chosen for one reason above all others: they can explain things clearly. It sounds obvious, but it is surprisingly rare. We have had sessions in the past where technically brilliant people presented information in a way that left the room more confused than when they arrived. We learnt from that. The facilitators you will hear from today have been tested in smaller settings first, given feedback, and iterated. What you are getting is a refined version, not a first draft.

The event is free. The knowledge is permanent. The registration takes thirty seconds. There is no reason not to.

title: Panel Discussion: Blockchain
description:
Most events on Blockchain are designed for people who already have a foundation and just want to go deeper. This one is different. AI & ML Club built this session specifically for the student who has heard the term a hundred times, nodded along in class, and quietly panicked when asked to actually do something with it. You are the target audience. There is no shame in being here at the beginning — there is only the question of what you choose to do about it. This is your practical starting point.

The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from Blockchain that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

One thing that consistently surprises attendees at AI & ML Club events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on Blockchain — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. They are a core part of what we are trying to create.

Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where Blockchain was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with Blockchain. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together.

After the event, all registered attendees will receive a curated resource pack: three links our facilitators actually use, two books they would recommend if pressed, and one honest assessment of the gaps in their own knowledge of Blockchain and how they are addressing them. We include the last one because we think intellectual honesty about what you do not know is as valuable as knowledge itself, and we want to model that for students.

The event is free. The knowledge is permanent. The registration takes thirty seconds. There is no reason not to.
