title: Data Structures Hackathon
description:
The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for Data Structures — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

The idea for this event on Data Structures came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

A few things we want to be transparent about. The facilitators running this session are not perfect. They will make mistakes in live demonstrations. When that happens, we will debug together, which is arguably the most educational part of any session. AI & ML Club believes in showing real work, not curated performances. If that sounds like a good use of your Saturday afternoon, we think you will find this event genuinely worthwhile.

After the event, all registered attendees will receive a curated resource pack: three links our facilitators actually use, two books they would recommend if pressed, and one honest assessment of the gaps in their own knowledge of Data Structures and how they are addressing them. We include the last one because we think intellectual honesty about what you do not know is as valuable as knowledge itself, and we want to model that for students.

Registration is open now. Space is limited. If you are on the fence, the fence is the wrong place to be.

title: DevOps — Guest Lecture
description:
A few things we want to be transparent about. The facilitators running this session are not perfect. They will make mistakes in live demonstrations. When that happens, we will debug together, which is arguably the most educational part of any session. Debate Society believes in showing real work, not curated performances. If that sounds like a good use of your Saturday afternoon, we think you will find this event genuinely worthwhile.

The idea for this event on DevOps came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

Here is what the session actually looks like. We open with a fifteen-minute orientation that covers the landscape of DevOps — where it sits relative to everything else you have learned, why it matters now more than it did five years ago, and what a working professional actually does with it on a Monday morning. This part is deliberately fast. We do not want to spend half the session on theory that you could have absorbed from a Wikipedia article. We want to get to the part where you do things.

We considered bringing in an external speaker for this one and decided against it. The best person to talk to RVCE students about navigating DevOps in the current environment is someone who was an RVCE student recently enough to remember what it felt like — and senior enough to have perspective on it. That is what we have. Someone who has been where you are, done what you are trying to do, and is willing to be honest about how they actually got there.

Certificates of participation will be issued to everyone who attends. We know that is a secondary concern for most people in this room, and we are glad for that. But for those who need it — for internship applications, for placement interviews, for anxious parents — it exists and it will arrive in your inbox within 48 hours of the event's close. Please register with your college email address to ensure delivery.

The event is free. The knowledge is permanent. The registration takes thirty seconds. There is no reason not to.

title: Blockchain — Guest Lecture
description:
A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with Blockchain professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. But if you are hoping for a deep technical dive at the cutting edge of the field, this is not that event. We are going for breadth and confidence-building, not depth. The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

Welcome to one of the most genuinely useful events Entrepreneurship Cell has run this academic year. We know that phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let us be specific about what we mean. This session on Blockchain was designed in response to direct feedback from students who sat placement interviews, bombed questions they had never been exposed to, and came back asking us to do something about it. We listened. What you will see today is the result of six weeks of curriculum design, two rounds of feedback from working engineers, and one very honest conversation about what actually matters.

The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from Blockchain that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

The person leading today's session on Blockchain was not our first choice — they were our third. Our first two choices were excellent but unavailable on this date. Our third choice turned out to be better than either of the first two, which is a useful reminder that the best facilitators are not always the most obvious ones. They bring a perspective on Blockchain that we had not fully anticipated when we reached out, and we think it makes the session richer for it.

Registration is open now. Space is limited. If you are on the fence, the fence is the wrong place to be.

title: Hands-on UI/UX Design Session
description:
The idea for this event on UI/UX Design came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

One thing that consistently surprises attendees at Quizzing Club events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on UI/UX Design — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. They are a core part of what we are trying to create.

The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for UI/UX Design — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

The speakers for this event have been chosen for one reason above all others: they can explain things clearly. It sounds obvious, but it is surprisingly rare. We have had sessions in the past where technically brilliant people presented information in a way that left the room more confused than when they arrived. We learnt from that. The facilitators you will hear from today have been tested in smaller settings first, given feedback, and iterated. What you are getting is a refined version, not a first draft.

After the event, all registered attendees will receive a curated resource pack: three links our facilitators actually use, two books they would recommend if pressed, and one honest assessment of the gaps in their own knowledge of UI/UX Design and how they are addressing them. We include the last one because we think intellectual honesty about what you do not know is as valuable as knowledge itself, and we want to model that for students.

If you have read this far and you are still not registered, we genuinely want to know what is stopping you. DM us on Instagram.

title: DevOps Showcase

title: Open Mic: Robotics & Automation
description:
One thing that consistently surprises attendees at Literary Club events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on Robotics & Automation — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. They are a core part of what we are trying to create.

We have structured this event around a principle that Literary Club cares about deeply: learning by producing, not learning by consuming. Every segment of this session on Robotics & Automation includes a moment where you must make something — a diagram, a line of code, a decision, a prediction. These are not graded. They will not be collected. They are for you, because the act of producing forces your brain to process information in a way that passive watching simply does not.

There is a version of this event that would have been easy to run — a polished slide deck, a speaker talking at you for ninety minutes, a group photo at the end. We chose not to do that version. Instead, the Literary Club spent the last month building a session on Robotics & Automation that puts you in the driver's seat from the first minute. The facilitators are here as guides, not lecturers. The agenda is a suggestion, not a script. And the only metric we care about at the end is whether you leave more capable than when you arrived.

Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where Robotics & Automation was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with Robotics & Automation. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together.

Show up. Work hard. Leave better. That is all we ask.

title: Open Source Contribution — Guest Lecture
description:
One thing that consistently surprises attendees at Astronomy Club events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on Open Source Contribution — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. They are a core part of what we are trying to create.

Here is what the session actually looks like. We open with a fifteen-minute orientation that covers the landscape of Open Source Contribution — where it sits relative to everything else you have learned, why it matters now more than it did five years ago, and what a working professional actually does with it on a Monday morning. This part is deliberately fast. We do not want to spend half the session on theory that you could have absorbed from a Wikipedia article. We want to get to the part where you do things.

Most events on Open Source Contribution are designed for people who already have a foundation and just want to go deeper. This one is different. Astronomy Club built this session specifically for the student who has heard the term a hundred times, nodded along in class, and quietly panicked when asked to actually do something with it. You are the target audience. There is no shame in being here at the beginning — there is only the question of what you choose to do about it. This is your practical starting point.

The person leading today's session on Open Source Contribution was not our first choice — they were our third. Our first two choices were excellent but unavailable on this date. Our third choice turned out to be better than either of the first two, which is a useful reminder that the best facilitators are not always the most obvious ones. They bring a perspective on Open Source Contribution that we had not fully anticipated when we reached out, and we think it makes the session richer for it.

We will see you there. Bring your laptop, bring your questions, and bring someone who needs this as much as you do.

title: Panel Discussion: React & Next.js
description:
Here is what the session actually looks like. We open with a fifteen-minute orientation that covers the landscape of React & Next.js — where it sits relative to everything else you have learned, why it matters now more than it did five years ago, and what a working professional actually does with it on a Monday morning. This part is deliberately fast. We do not want to spend half the session on theory that you could have absorbed from a Wikipedia article. We want to get to the part where you do things.

The idea for this event on React & Next.js came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

We want to be upfront about what this event is not. It is not a placement coaching session. It is not a certificate farm. It is not a box to tick on your co-curricular activity sheet. It is a room full of people who are genuinely curious about React & Next.js, facilitated by people who have invested real time in understanding it, with the goal of leaving everyone slightly less confused than they arrived. If that sounds like a good way to spend a few hours, the door is open.

Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where React & Next.js was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with React & Next.js. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together.

The venue has been chosen specifically for its layout. We needed a room where the facilitator could move around freely, where breakout discussions could happen without disrupting the main session, and where the acoustics would not turn every explanation into an echo. We did a walkthrough last week. The space works. If you have attended events at other venues and found them frustrating for these reasons, this one should be different.

This is Debate Society's commitment: if you attend and feel it was not worth your time, tell us directly. We will listen and we will fix it for next time. That is how we have gotten better every semester.

title: DevOps Showcase
description:
A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with DevOps professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. But if you are hoping for a deep technical dive at the cutting edge of the field, this is not that event. We are going for breadth and confidence-building, not depth. The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from DevOps that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

Most events on DevOps are designed for people who already have a foundation and just want to go deeper. This one is different. Coding Club RVCE built this session specifically for the student who has heard the term a hundred times, nodded along in class, and quietly panicked when asked to actually do something with it. You are the target audience. There is no shame in being here at the beginning — there is only the question of what you choose to do about it. This is your practical starting point.

The person leading today's session on DevOps was not our first choice — they were our third. Our first two choices were excellent but unavailable on this date. Our third choice turned out to be better than either of the first two, which is a useful reminder that the best facilitators are not always the most obvious ones. They bring a perspective on DevOps that we had not fully anticipated when we reached out, and we think it makes the session richer for it.

The venue has been chosen specifically for its layout. We needed a room where the facilitator could move around freely, where breakout discussions could happen without disrupting the main session, and where the acoustics would not turn every explanation into an echo. We did a walkthrough last week. The space works. If you have attended events at other venues and found them frustrating for these reasons, this one should be different.

Registration is open now. Space is limited. If you are on the fence, the fence is the wrong place to be.

title: Industry Talk: Open Source Contribution
description:
One thing that consistently surprises attendees at IEEE Student Branch events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on Open Source Contribution — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. They are a core part of what we are trying to create.

Most events on Open Source Contribution are designed for people who already have a foundation and just want to go deeper. This one is different. IEEE Student Branch built this session specifically for the student who has heard the term a hundred times, nodded along in class, and quietly panicked when asked to actually do something with it. You are the target audience. There is no shame in being here at the beginning — there is only the question of what you choose to do about it. This is your practical starting point.

The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for Open Source Contribution — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

The speakers for this event have been chosen for one reason above all others: they can explain things clearly. It sounds obvious, but it is surprisingly rare. We have had sessions in the past where technically brilliant people presented information in a way that left the room more confused than when they arrived. We learnt from that. The facilitators you will hear from today have been tested in smaller settings first, given feedback, and iterated. What you are getting is a refined version, not a first draft.

Certificates of participation will be issued to everyone who attends. We know that is a secondary concern for most people in this room, and we are glad for that. But for those who need it — for internship applications, for placement interviews, for anxious parents — it exists and it will arrive in your inbox within 48 hours of the event's close. Please register with your college email address to ensure delivery.

We will see you there. Bring your laptop, bring your questions, and bring someone who needs this as much as you do.

description:

Welcome to one of the most genuinely useful events AI & ML Club has run this academic year. We know that phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let us be specific about what we mean. This session on Blockchain was designed in response to direct feedback from students who sat placement interviews, bombed questions they had never been exposed to, and came back asking us to do something about it. We listened. What you will see today is the result of six weeks of curriculum design, two rounds of feedback from working engineers, and one very honest conversation about what actually matters.

Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where Blockchain was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with Blockchain. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together.

After the event, all registered attendees will receive a curated resource pack: three links our facilitators actually use, two books they would recommend if pressed, and one honest assessment of the gaps in their own knowledge of Blockchain and how they are addressing them. We include the last one because we think intellectual honesty about what you do not know is as valuable as knowledge itself, and we want to model that for students.

We will see you there. Bring your laptop, bring your questions, and bring someone who needs this as much as you do.

title: Seminar on Cybersecurity
description:
We want to be upfront about what this event is not. It is not a placement coaching session. It is not a certificate farm. It is not a box to tick on your co-curricular activity sheet. It is a room full of people who are genuinely curious about Cybersecurity, facilitated by people who have invested real time in understanding it, with the goal of leaving everyone slightly less confused than they arrived. If that sounds like a good way to spend a few hours, the door is open.

The idea for this event on Cybersecurity came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from Cybersecurity that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

The speakers for this event have been chosen for one reason above all others: they can explain things clearly. It sounds obvious, but it is surprisingly rare. We have had sessions in the past where technically brilliant people presented information in a way that left the room more confused than when they arrived. We learnt from that. The facilitators you will hear from today have been tested in smaller settings first, given feedback, and iterated. What you are getting is a refined version, not a first draft.

Food and drinks will be available throughout. We mention this not to bribe you into attending — the content should do that — but because we have noticed that sessions run better when people are not hungry. Please eat something before you arrive as well. A three-hour session on Cybersecurity on an empty stomach is not the optimal learning environment, and we speak from experience.

title: Competitive Programming — Guest Lecture
description:
The idea for this event on Competitive Programming came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from Competitive Programming that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

One thing that consistently surprises attendees at Drama Club events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on Competitive Programming — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. They are a core part of what we are trying to create.

After the event, all registered attendees will receive a curated resource pack: three links our facilitators actually use, two books they would recommend if pressed, and one honest assessment of the gaps in their own knowledge of Competitive Programming and how they are addressing them. We include the last one because we think intellectual honesty about what you do not know is as valuable as knowledge itself, and we want to model that for students.

Show up. Work hard. Leave better. That is all we ask.

title: Game Development Hackathon
description:
One thing that consistently surprises attendees at AI & ML Club events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on Game Development — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. They are a core part of what we are trying to create.

The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from Game Development that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

The idea for this event on Game Development came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

We considered bringing in an external speaker for this one and decided against it. The best person to talk to RVCE students about navigating Game Development in the current environment is someone who was an RVCE student recently enough to remember what it felt like — and senior enough to have perspective on it. That is what we have. Someone who has been where you are, done what you are trying to do, and is willing to be honest about how they actually got there.

Certificates of participation will be issued to everyone who attends. We know that is a secondary concern for most people in this room, and we are glad for that. But for those who need it — for internship applications, for placement interviews, for anxious parents — it exists and it will arrive in your inbox within 48 hours of the event's close. Please register with your college email address to ensure delivery.

This is AI & ML Club's commitment: if you attend and feel it was not worth your time, tell us directly. We will listen and we will fix it for next time. That is how we have gotten better every semester.

title: Game Development Hackathon
description:
We have structured this event around a principle that Design Guild cares about deeply: learning by producing, not learning by consuming. Every segment of this session on Game Development includes a moment where you must make something — a diagram, a line of code, a decision, a prediction. These are not graded. They will not be collected. They are for you, because the act of producing forces your brain to process information in a way that passive watching simply does not.

Most events on Game Development are designed for people who already have a foundation and just want to go deeper. This one is different. Design Guild built this session specifically for the student who has heard the term a hundred times, nodded along in class, and quietly panicked when asked to actually do something with it. You are the target audience. There is no shame in being here at the beginning — there is only the question of what you choose to do about it. This is your practical starting point.

After the event, all registered attendees will receive a curated resource pack: three links our facilitators actually use, two books they would recommend if pressed, and one honest assessment of the gaps in their own knowledge of Game Development and how they are addressing them. title: Research Methodology 101: Beginner's Guide
description:
One thing that consistently surprises attendees at Sports Council events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on Research Methodology — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. They are a core part of what we are trying to create.

The idea for this event on Research Methodology came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for Research Methodology — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

This is Sports Council's commitment: if you attend and feel it was not worth your time, tell us directly. We will listen and we will fix it for next time. That is how we have gotten better every semester.

title: Career Fair: Blockchain
description:
A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with Blockchain professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. But if you are hoping for a deep technical dive at the cutting edge of the field, this is not that event. We are going for breadth and confidence-building, not depth. The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

Most events on Blockchain are designed for people who already have a foundation and just want to go deeper. This one is different. Coding Club RVCE built this session specifically for the student who has heard the term a hundred times, nodded along in class, and quietly panicked when asked to actually do something with it. You are the target audience. There is no shame in being here at the beginning — there is only the question of what you choose to do about it. This is your practical starting point.

We have structured this event around a principle that Coding Club RVCE cares about deeply: learning by producing, not learning by consuming. Every segment of this session on Blockchain includes a moment where you must make something — a diagram, a line of code, a decision, a prediction. These are not graded. They will not be collected. They are for you, because the act of producing forces your brain to process information in a way that passive watching simply does not.

The person leading today's session on Blockchain was not our first choice — they were our third. Our first two choices were excellent but unavailable on this date. Our third choice turned out to be better than either of the first two, which is a useful reminder that the best facilitators are not always the most obvious ones. They bring a perspective on Blockchain that we had not fully anticipated when we reached out, and we think it makes the session richer for it.

Food and drinks will be available throughout. We mention this not to bribe you into attending — the content should do that — but because we have noticed that sessions run better when people are not hungry. Please eat something before you arrive as well. A three-hour session on Blockchain on an empty stomach is not the optimal learning environment, and we speak from experience.

This is Coding Club RVCE's commitment: if you attend and feel it was not worth your time, tell us directly. We will listen and we will fix it for next time. That is how we have gotten better every semester.

But if you are hoping for a deep technical dive at the cutting edge of the field, this is not that event. We are going for breadth and confidence-building, not depth. The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where Python for Beginners was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with Python for Beginners. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together.

After the event, all registered attendees will receive a curated resource pack: three links our facilitators actually use, two books they would recommend if pressed, and one honest assessment of the gaps in their own knowledge of Python for Beginners and how they are addressing them. title: Data Structures Bootcamp
description:
There is a version of this event that would have been easy to run — a polished slide deck, a speaker talking at you for ninety minutes, a group photo at the end. We chose not to do that version. Instead, the Open Source Club spent the last month building a session on Data Structures that puts you in the driver's seat from the first minute. The facilitators are here as guides, not lecturers. The agenda is a suggestion, not a script. And the only metric we care about at the end is whether you leave more capable than when you arrived.

We want to be upfront about what this event is not. It is not a placement coaching session. It is not a certificate farm. It is not a box to tick on your co-curricular activity sheet. It is a room full of people who are genuinely curious about Data Structures, facilitated by people who have invested real time in understanding it, with the goal of leaving everyone slightly less confused than they arrived. If that sounds like a good way to spend a few hours, the door is open.

The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for Data Structures — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where Data Structures was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with Data Structures. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together.

Food and drinks will be available throughout. We mention this not to bribe you into attending — the content should do that — but because we have noticed that sessions run better when people are not hungry. Please eat something before you arrive as well. A three-hour session on Data Structures on an empty stomach is not the optimal learning environment, and we speak from experience.

This is Open Source Club's commitment: if you attend and feel it was not worth your time, tell us directly. We will listen and we will fix it for next time. That is how we have gotten better every semester.

title: Blockchain Bootcamp
description:
One thing that consistently surprises attendees at Open Source Club events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on Blockchain — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. They are a core part of what we are trying to create.

The idea for this event on Blockchain came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

Here is what the session actually looks like. We open with a fifteen-minute orientation that covers the landscape of Blockchain — where it sits relative to everything else you have learned, why it matters now more than it did five years ago, and what a working professional actually does with it on a Monday morning. This part is deliberately fast. We do not want to spend half the session on theory that you could have absorbed from a Wikipedia article. We want to get to the part where you do things.

Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where Blockchain was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with Blockchain. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together.

After the event, all registered attendees will receive a curated resource pack: three links our facilitators actually use, two books they would recommend if pressed, and one honest assessment of the gaps in their own knowledge of Blockchain and how they are addressing them. We include the last one because we think intellectual honesty about what you do not know is as valuable as knowledge itself, and we want to model that for students.

This is Open Source Club's commitment: if you attend and feel it was not worth your time, tell us directly. We will listen and we will fix it for next time. That is how we have gotten better every semester.

title: Web Dev Workshop: Machine Learning
description:
Here is what the session actually looks like. We open with a fifteen-minute orientation that covers the landscape of Machine Learning — where it sits relative to everything else you have learned, why it matters now more than it did five years ago, and what a working professional actually does with it on a Monday morning. This part is deliberately fast. We do not want to spend half the session on theory that you could have absorbed from a Wikipedia article. We want to get to the part where you do things.

Welcome to one of the most genuinely useful events Literary Club has run this academic year. We know that phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let us be specific about what we mean. This session on Machine Learning was designed in response to direct feedback from students who sat placement interviews, bombed questions they had never been exposed to, and came back asking us to do something about it. We listened. What you will see today is the result of six weeks of curriculum design, two rounds of feedback from working engineers, and one very honest conversation about what actually matters.

We want to be upfront about what this event is not. It is not a placement coaching session. It is not a certificate farm. It is not a box to tick on your co-curricular activity sheet. It is a room full of people who are genuinely curious about Machine Learning, facilitated by people who have invested real time in understanding it, with the goal of leaving everyone slightly less confused than they arrived. If that sounds like a good way to spend a few hours, the door is open.

The person leading today's session on Machine Learning was not our first choice — they were our third. Our first two choices were excellent but unavailable on this date. Our third choice turned out to be better than either of the first two, which is a useful reminder that the best facilitators are not always the most obvious ones. They bring a perspective on Machine Learning that we had not fully anticipated when we reached out, and we think it makes the session richer for it.

This is Literary Club's commitment: if you attend and feel it was not worth your time, tell us directly. We will listen and we will fix it for next time. That is how we have gotten better every semester.

title: Robotics & Automation 101: Beginner's Guide
description:
We have structured this event around a principle that Music Society cares about deeply: learning by producing, not learning by consuming. Every segment of this session on Robotics & Automation includes a moment where you must make something — a diagram, a line of code, a decision, a prediction. These are not graded. They will not be collected. They are for you, because the act of producing forces your brain to process information in a way that passive watching simply does not.

The idea for this event on Robotics & Automation came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with Robotics & Automation professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. But if you are hoping for a deep technical dive at the cutting edge of the field, this is not that event. We are going for breadth and confidence-building, not depth. The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

Certificates of participation will be issued to everyone who attends. We know that is a secondary concern for most people in this room, and we are glad for that. But for those who need it — for internship applications, for placement interviews, for anxious parents — it exists and it will arrive in your inbox within 48 hours of the event's close. Please register with your college email address to ensure delivery.

This is Music Society's commitment: if you attend and feel it was not worth your time, tell us directly. We will listen and we will fix it for next time. That is how we have gotten better every semester.

title: Annual Photography Basics Competition
description:
The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from Photography Basics that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

There is a version of this event that would have been easy to run — a polished slide deck, a speaker talking at you for ninety minutes, a group photo at the end. We chose not to do that version. Instead, the Coding Club RVCE spent the last month building a session on Photography Basics that puts you in the driver's seat from the first minute. The facilitators are here as guides, not lecturers. The agenda is a suggestion, not a script. And the only metric we care about at the end is whether you leave more capable than when you arrived.

A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with Photography Basics professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. But if you are hoping for a deep technical dive at the cutting edge of the field, this is not that event. We are going for breadth and confidence-building, not depth. The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

We considered bringing in an external speaker for this one and decided against it. The best person to talk to RVCE students about navigating Photography Basics in the current environment is someone who was an RVCE student recently enough to remember what it felt like — and senior enough to have perspective on it. That is what we have. Someone who has been where you are, done what you are trying to do, and is willing to be honest about how they actually got there.

Food and drinks will be available throughout. We mention this not to bribe you into attending — the content should do that — but because we have noticed that sessions run better when people are not hungry. Please eat something before you arrive as well. A three-hour session on Photography Basics on an empty stomach is not the optimal learning environment, and we speak from experience.

Show up. Work hard. Leave better. That is all we ask.

A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with System Design professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. But if you are hoping for a deep technical dive at the cutting edge of the field, this is not that event. We are going for breadth and confidence-building, not depth. The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for System Design — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

Most events on System Design are designed for people who already have a foundation and just want to go deeper. This one is different. Open Source Club built this session specifically for the student who has heard the term a hundred times, nodded along in class, and quietly panicked when asked to actually do something with it. You are the target audience. There is no shame in being here at the beginning — there is only the question of what you choose to do about it. This is your practical starting point.

We considered bringing in an external speaker for this one and decided against it. The best person to talk to RVCE students about navigating System Design in the current environment is someone who was an RVCE student recently enough to remember what it felt like — and senior enough to have perspective on it. That is what we have. Someone who has been where you are, done what you are trying to do, and is willing to be honest about how they actually got there.

The venue has been chosen specifically for its layout. We needed a room where the facilitator could move around freely, where breakout discussions could happen without disrupting the main session, and where the acoustics would not turn every explanation into an echo. We did a walkthrough last week. The space works. If you have attended events at other venues and found them frustrating for these reasons, this one should be different.

Show up. Work hard. Leave better. That is all we ask.

title: Seminar on IoT Projects
description:
Here is what the session actually looks like. We open with a fifteen-minute orientation that covers the landscape of IoT Projects — where it sits relative to everything else you have learned, why it matters now more than it did five years ago, and what a working professional actually does with it on a Monday morning. This part is deliberately fast. We do not want to spend half the session on theory that you could have absorbed from a Wikipedia article. We want to get to the part where you do things.

One thing that consistently surprises attendees at Coding Club RVCE events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on IoT Projects — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. They are a core part of what we are trying to create.

There is a version of this event that would have been easy to run — a polished slide deck, a speaker talking at you for ninety minutes, a group photo at the end. We chose not to do that version. Instead, the Coding Club RVCE spent the last month building a session on IoT Projects that puts you in the driver's seat from the first minute. The facilitators are here as guides, not lecturers. The agenda is a suggestion, not a script. And the only metric we care about at the end is whether you leave more capable than when you arrived.

We considered bringing in an external speaker for this one and decided against it. The best person to talk to RVCE students about navigating IoT Projects in the current environment is someone who was an RVCE student recently enough to remember what it felt like — and senior enough to have perspective on it. That is what we have. Someone who has been where you are, done what you are trying to do, and is willing to be honest about how they actually got there.

Food and drinks will be available throughout. We mention this not to bribe you into attending — the content should do that — but because we have noticed that sessions run better when people are not hungry. Please eat something before you arrive as well. A three-hour session on IoT Projects on an empty stomach is not the optimal learning environment, and we speak from experience.

The event is free. The knowledge is permanent. The registration takes thirty seconds. There is no reason not to.

title: Career Fair: Robotics & Automation
description:

Then we introduce the concept from Robotics & Automation that solves it. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

We considered bringing in an external speaker for this one and decided against it. The best person to talk to RVCE students about navigating Data Structures in the current environment is someone who was an RVCE student recently enough to remember what it felt like — and senior enough to have perspective on it. That is what we have. Someone who has been where you are, done what you are trying to do, and is willing to be honest about how they actually got there.

After the event, all registered attendees will receive a curated resource pack: three links our facilitators actually use, two books they would recommend if pressed, and one honest assessment of the gaps in their own knowledge of Data Structures and how they are addressing them. We include the last one because we think intellectual honesty about what you do not know is as valuable as knowledge itself, and we want to model that for students.

Show up. Work hard. Leave better. That is all we ask.

title: Open Source Contribution Sprint
description:
The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from Open Source Contribution that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

One thing that consistently surprises attendees at Literary Club events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on Open Source Contribution — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. They are a core part of what we are trying to create.

There is a version of this event that would have been easy to run — a polished slide deck, a speaker talking at you for ninety minutes, a group photo at the end. We chose not to do that version. Instead, the Literary Club spent the last month building a session on Open Source Contribution that puts you in the driver's seat from the first minute. The facilitators are here as guides, not lecturers. The agenda is a suggestion, not a script. And the only metric we care about at the end is whether you leave more capable than when you arrived.

The speakers for this event have been chosen for one reason above all others: they can explain things clearly. It sounds obvious, but it is surprisingly rare. We have had sessions in the past where technically brilliant people presented information in a way that left the room more confused than when they arrived. We learnt from that. The facilitators you will hear from today have been tested in smaller settings first, given feedback, and iterated. What you are getting is a refined version, not a first draft.

The venue has been chosen specifically for its layout. We needed a room where the facilitator could move around freely, where breakout discussions could happen without disrupting the main session, and where the acoustics would not turn every explanation into an echo. We did a walkthrough last week. The space works. If you have attended events at other venues and found them frustrating for these reasons, this one should be different.

If you have read this far and you are still not registered, we genuinely want to know what is stopping you. DM us on Instagram.

title: System Design — Guest Lecture
description:
The idea for this event on System Design came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

Here is what the session actually looks like. We open with a fifteen-minute orientation that covers the landscape of System Design — where it sits relative to everything else you have learned, why it matters now more than it did five years ago, and what a working professional actually does with it on a Monday morning. This part is deliberately fast. We do not want to spend half the session on theory that you could have absorbed from a Wikipedia article. We want to get to the part where you do things.

A few things we want to be transparent about. The facilitators running this session are not perfect. They will make mistakes in live demonstrations. When that happens, we will debug together, which is arguably the most educational part of any session. Cultural Committee believes in showing real work, not curated performances. If that sounds like a good use of your Saturday afternoon, we think you will find this event genuinely worthwhile.

Show up. Work hard. Leave better. That is all we ask.

title: Hands-on Public Speaking Session
description: We asked our alumni what one topic they wish they had learned before their first internship. Public Speaking came up more than any other. So here we are. Expect a mix of rapid-fire slides (kept to 15 minutes maximum), live work on real codebases, and breakout discussions in small groups. The primary takeaway is not a certificate — it is a working mental model of Public Speaking that will help you read code, debug faster, and ask better questions in interviews. This one will be worth the two hours. Promise.

title: UI/UX Design Bootcamp
description:
There is a version of this event that would have been easy to run — a polished slide deck, a speaker talking at you for ninety minutes, a group photo at the end. We chose not to do that version. Instead, the Drama Club spent the last month building a session on UI/UX Design that puts you in the driver's seat from the first minute. The facilitators are here as guides, not lecturers. The agenda is a suggestion, not a script. And the only metric we care about at the end is whether you leave more capable than when you arrived.

We want to be upfront about what this event is not. It is not a placement coaching session. It is not a certificate farm. It is not a box to tick on your co-curricular activity sheet. It is a room full of people who are genuinely curious about UI/UX Design, facilitated by people who have invested real time in understanding it, with the goal of leaving everyone slightly less confused than they arrived. If that sounds like a good way to spend a few hours, the door is open.

The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from UI/UX Design that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

The speakers for this event have been chosen for one reason above all others: they can explain things clearly. It sounds obvious, but it is surprisingly rare. We have had sessions in the past where technically brilliant people presented information in a way that left the room more confused than when they arrived. We learnt from that. The facilitators you will hear from today have been tested in smaller settings first, given feedback, and iterated. What you are getting is a refined version, not a first draft.

After the event, all registered attendees will receive a curated resource pack: three links our facilitators actually use, two books they would recommend if pressed, and one honest assessment of the gaps in their own knowledge of UI/UX Design and how they are addressing them. We include the last one because we think intellectual honesty about what you do not know is as valuable as knowledge itself, and we want to model that for students.

Show up. Work hard. Leave better. That is all we ask.

title: DevOps Bootcamp
description:
Welcome to one of the most genuinely useful events Finance Club has run this academic year. We know that phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let us be specific about what we mean. This session on DevOps was designed in response to direct feedback from students who sat placement interviews, bombed questions they had never been exposed to, and came back asking us to do something about it. We listened. What you will see today is the result of six weeks of curriculum design, two rounds of feedback from working engineers, and one very honest conversation about what actually matters.

The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for DevOps — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with DevOps professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. But if you are hoping for a deep technical dive at the cutting edge of the field, this is not that event. We are going for breadth and confidence-building, not depth. The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where DevOps was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with DevOps. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together.

After the event, all registered attendees will receive a curated resource pack: three links our facilitators actually use, two books they would recommend if pressed, and one honest assessment of the gaps in their own knowledge of DevOps and how they are addressing them. We include the last one because we think intellectual honesty about what you do not know is as valuable as knowledge itself, and we want to model that for students.

The event is free. The knowledge is permanent. The registration takes thirty seconds. There is no reason not to.

We want to be upfront about what this event is not. It is not a placement coaching session. It is not a certificate farm. It is not a box to tick on your co-curricular activity sheet. It is a room full of people who are genuinely curious about IoT Projects, facilitated by people who have invested real time in understanding it, with the goal of leaving everyone slightly less confused than they arrived. If that sounds like a good way to spend a few hours, the door is open.

There is a version of this event that would have been easy to run — a polished slide deck, a speaker talking at you for ninety minutes, a group photo at the end. We chose not to do that version. Instead, the Placement Cell spent the last month building a session on IoT Projects that puts you in the driver's seat from the first minute. The facilitators are here as guides, not lecturers. The agenda is a suggestion, not a script. And the only metric we care about at the end is whether you leave more capable than when you arrived.

The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for IoT Projects — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

The person leading today's session on IoT Projects was not our first choice — they were our third. Our first two choices were excellent but unavailable on this date. Our third choice turned out to be better than either of the first two, which is a useful reminder that the best facilitators are not always the most obvious ones. They bring a perspective on IoT Projects that we had not fully anticipated when we reached out, and we think it makes the session richer for it.

If you have read this far and you are still not registered, we genuinely want to know what is stopping you. DM us on Instagram.

description:

In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where Public Speaking was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with Public Speaking. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together.

Show up. Work hard. Leave better. That is all we ask.

title: Web Dev Workshop: IoT Projects
description:
Welcome to one of the most genuinely useful events Cybersecurity Club has run this academic year. We know that phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let us be specific about what we mean. This session on IoT Projects was designed in response to direct feedback from students who sat placement interviews, bombed questions they had never been exposed to, and came back asking us to do something about it. We listened. What you will see today is the result of six weeks of curriculum design, two rounds of feedback from working engineers, and one very honest conversation about what actually matters.

One thing that consistently surprises attendees at Cybersecurity Club events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on IoT Projects — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. They are a core part of what we are trying to create.

Here is what the session actually looks like. We open with a fifteen-minute orientation that covers the landscape of IoT Projects — where it sits relative to everything else you have learned, why it matters now more than it did five years ago, and what a working professional actually does with it on a Monday morning. This part is deliberately fast. We do not want to spend half the session on theory that you could have absorbed from a Wikipedia article. We want to get to the part where you do things.

The speakers for this event have been chosen for one reason above all others: they can explain things clearly. It sounds obvious, but it is surprisingly rare. We have had sessions in the past where technically brilliant people presented information in a way that left the room more confused than when they arrived. We learnt from that. The facilitators you will hear from today have been tested in smaller settings first, given feedback, and iterated. What you are getting is a refined version, not a first draft.

After the event, all registered attendees will receive a curated resource pack: three links our facilitators actually use, two books they would recommend if pressed, and one honest assessment of the gaps in their own knowledge of IoT Projects and how they are addressing them. We include the last one because we think intellectual honesty about what you do not know is as valuable as knowledge itself, and we want to model that for students.

Show up. Work hard. Leave better. That is all we ask.

This session on Photography Basics was designed in response to direct feedback from students who sat placement interviews, bombed questions they had never been exposed to, and came back asking us to do something about it. We listened. What you will see today is the result of six weeks of curriculum design, two rounds of feedback from working engineers, and one very honest conversation about what actually matters.

One thing that consistently surprises attendees at AI & ML Club events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on Photography Basics — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. They are a core part of what we are trying to create.

The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for Photography Basics — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

The person leading today's session on Photography Basics was not our first choice — they were our third. Our first two choices were excellent but unavailable on this date. Our third choice turned out to be better than either of the first two, which is a useful reminder that the best facilitators are not always the most obvious ones. They bring a perspective on Photography Basics that we had not fully anticipated when we reached out, and we think it makes the session richer for it.

Food and drinks will be available throughout. We mention this not to bribe you into attending — the content should do that — but because we have noticed that sessions run better when people are not hungry. Please eat something before you arrive as well. A three-hour session on Photography Basics on an empty stomach is not the optimal learning environment, and we speak from experience.

Registration is open now. Space is limited. If you are on the fence, the fence is the wrong place to be.

title: Networking Night: Cybersecurity
description:
The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from Cybersecurity that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

Most events on Cybersecurity are designed for people who already have a foundation and just want to go deeper. This one is different. Literary Club built this session specifically for the student who has heard the term a hundred times, nodded along in class, and quietly panicked when asked to actually do something with it. You are the target audience. There is no shame in being here at the beginning — there is only the question of what you choose to do about it. This is your practical starting point.

It is a room full of people who are genuinely curious about Cybersecurity, facilitated by people who have invested real time in understanding it, with the goal of leaving everyone slightly less confused than they arrived. If that sounds like a good way to spend a few hours, the door is open.

Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where Cybersecurity was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with Cybersecurity. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together.

If you have read this far and you are still not registered, we genuinely want to know what is stopping you. DM us on Instagram.

title: Finance 101 — Guest Lecture
description:
One thing that consistently surprises attendees at Open Source Club events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. They are a core part of what we are trying to create.

Welcome to one of the most genuinely useful events Open Source Club has run this academic year. We know that phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let us be specific about what we mean. This session on Finance 101 was designed in response to direct feedback from students who sat placement interviews, bombed questions they had never been exposed to, and came back asking us to do something about it. We considered bringing in an external speaker for this one and decided against it. The best person to talk to RVCE students about navigating Finance 101 in the current environment is someone who was an RVCE student recently enough to remember what it felt like — and senior enough to have perspective on it. That is what we have. Someone who has been where you are, done what you are trying to do, and is willing to be honest about how they actually got there.

We will see you there. Bring your laptop, bring your questions, and bring someone who needs this as much as you do.
