title: Web Dev Workshop: Blockchain
description:
A few things we want to be transparent about. The facilitators running this session are not perfect. They will make mistakes in live demonstrations. When that happens, we will debug together, which is arguably the most educational part of any session. Open Source Club believes in showing real work, not curated performances. If that sounds like a good use of your Saturday afternoon, we think you will find this event genuinely worthwhile.

Most events on Blockchain are designed for people who already have a foundation and just want to go deeper. This one is different. Open Source Club built this session specifically for the student who has heard the term a hundred times, nodded along in class, and quietly panicked when asked to actually do something with it. You are the target audience. There is no shame in being here at the beginning — there is only the question of what you choose to do about it. This is your practical starting point.

The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for Blockchain — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

Certificates of participation will be issued to everyone who attends. We know that is a secondary concern for most people in this room, and we are glad for that. But for those who need it — for internship applications, for placement interviews, for anxious parents — it exists and it will arrive in your inbox within 48 hours of the event's close. Please register with your college email address to ensure delivery.

The event is free. The knowledge is permanent. The registration takes thirty seconds. There is no reason not to.

Most events on REST APIs are designed for people who already have a foundation and just want to go deeper. This one is different. Sports Council built this session specifically for the student who has heard the term a hundred times, nodded along in class, and quietly panicked when asked to actually do something with it. You are the target audience. There is no shame in being here at the beginning — there is only the question of what you choose to do about it. This is your practical starting point.

Here is what the session actually looks like. We open with a fifteen-minute orientation that covers the landscape of REST APIs — where it sits relative to everything else you have learned, why it matters now more than it did five years ago, and what a working professional actually does with it on a Monday morning. This part is deliberately fast. We do not want to spend half the session on theory that you could have absorbed from a Wikipedia article. We want to get to the part where you do things.

A few things we want to be transparent about. The facilitators running this session are not perfect. They will make mistakes in live demonstrations. When that happens, we will debug together, which is arguably the most educational part of any session. Sports Council believes in showing real work, not curated performances. If that sounds like a good use of your Saturday afternoon, we think you will find this event genuinely worthwhile.

The speakers for this event have been chosen for one reason above all others: they can explain things clearly. It sounds obvious, but it is surprisingly rare. We have had sessions in the past where technically brilliant people presented information in a way that left the room more confused than when they arrived. We learnt from that. The facilitators you will hear from today have been tested in smaller settings first, given feedback, and iterated. What you are getting is a refined version, not a first draft.

Certificates of participation will be issued to everyone who attends. We know that is a secondary concern for most people in this room, and we are glad for that. But for those who need it — for internship applications, for placement interviews, for anxious parents — it exists and it will arrive in your inbox within 48 hours of the event's close. Please register with your college email address to ensure delivery.

If you have read this far and you are still not registered, we genuinely want to know what is stopping you. DM us on Instagram.

title: Annual IoT Projects Competition
description:
We want to be upfront about what this event is not. It is not a placement coaching session. It is not a certificate farm. It is not a box to tick on your co-curricular activity sheet. Robotics Club built this session specifically for the student who has heard the term a hundred times, nodded along in class, and quietly panicked when asked to actually do something with it. Seats will run out before the deadline does. Register now.

title: Annual Robotics & Automation Competition
description:
A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with Robotics & Automation professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. But if you are hoping for a deep technical dive at the cutting edge of the field, this is not that event. We are going for breadth and confidence-building, not depth. The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from Robotics & Automation that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

Most events on Robotics & Automation are designed for people who already have a foundation and just want to go deeper. This one is different. Finance Club built this session specifically for the student who has heard the term a hundred times, nodded along in class, and quietly panicked when asked to actually do something with it. You are the target audience. There is no shame in being here at the beginning — there is only the question of what you choose to do about it. This is your practical starting point.

Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where Robotics & Automation was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with Robotics & Automation. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together.

Food and drinks will be available throughout. We mention this not to bribe you into attending — the content should do that — but because we have noticed that sessions run better when people are not hungry. Please eat something before you arrive as well. A three-hour session on Robotics & Automation on an empty stomach is not the optimal learning environment, and we speak from experience.

Registration is open now. Space is limited. If you are on the fence, the fence is the wrong place to be.

title: UI/UX Design 101: Beginner's Guide
description: The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from UI/UX Design that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday. The idea for this event on UI/UX Design came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews. One thing that consistently surprises attendees at Coding Club RVCE events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on UI/UX Design — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. They are a core part of what we are trying to create. The speakers for this event have been chosen for one reason above all others: they can explain things clearly. It sounds obvious, but it is surprisingly rare. We have had sessions in the past where technically brilliant people presented information in a way that left the room more confused than when they arrived. We learnt from that. The facilitators you will hear from today have been tested in smaller settings first, given feedback, and iterated. What you are getting is a refined version, not a first draft. Certificates of participation will be issued to everyone who attends. We know that is a secondary concern for most people in this room, and we are glad for that. But for those who need it — for internship applications, for placement interviews, for anxious parents — it exists and it will arrive in your inbox within 48 hours of the event's close. title: Industry Talk: Career Prep & Placement
description:
The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for Career Prep & Placement — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

One thing that consistently surprises attendees at Music Society events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on Career Prep & Placement — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. They are a core part of what we are trying to create.

Welcome to one of the most genuinely useful events Music Society has run this academic year. We know that phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let us be specific about what we mean. This session on Career Prep & Placement was designed in response to direct feedback from students who sat placement interviews, bombed questions they had never been exposed to, and came back asking us to do something about it. We listened. What you will see today is the result of six weeks of curriculum design, two rounds of feedback from working engineers, and one very honest conversation about what actually matters.

After the event, all registered attendees will receive a curated resource pack: three links our facilitators actually use, two books they would recommend if pressed, and one honest assessment of the gaps in their own knowledge of Career Prep & Placement and how they are addressing them. We include the last one because we think intellectual honesty about what you do not know is as valuable as knowledge itself, and we want to model that for students.

This is Music Society's commitment: if you attend and feel it was not worth your time, tell us directly. We will listen and we will fix it for next time. That is how we have gotten better every semester.

title: Networking Night: UI/UX Design
description:
Welcome to one of the most genuinely useful events Placement Cell has run this academic year. We know that phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let us be specific about what we mean. This session on UI/UX Design was designed in response to direct feedback from students who sat placement interviews, bombed questions they had never been exposed to, and came back asking us to do something about it. We listened. What you will see today is the result of six weeks of curriculum design, two rounds of feedback from working engineers, and one very honest conversation about what actually matters.

We want to be upfront about what this event is not. It is not a placement coaching session. It is not a certificate farm. It is not a box to tick on your co-curricular activity sheet. It is a room full of people who are genuinely curious about UI/UX Design, facilitated by people who have invested real time in understanding it, with the goal of leaving everyone slightly less confused than they arrived. If that sounds like a good way to spend a few hours, the door is open.

Every segment of this session on UI/UX Design includes a moment where you must make something — a diagram, a line of code, a decision, a prediction. These are not graded. They will not be collected. They are for you, because the act of producing forces your brain to process information in a way that passive watching simply does not.

The person leading today's session on UI/UX Design was not our first choice — they were our third. Our first two choices were excellent but unavailable on this date. Our third choice turned out to be better than either of the first two, which is a useful reminder that the best facilitators are not always the most obvious ones. They bring a perspective on UI/UX Design that we had not fully anticipated when we reached out, and we think it makes the session richer for it.

After the event, all registered attendees will receive a curated resource pack: three links our facilitators actually use, two books they would recommend if pressed, and one honest assessment of the gaps in their own knowledge of UI/UX Design and how they are addressing them. We include the last one because we think intellectual honesty about what you do not know is as valuable as knowledge itself, and we want to model that for students.

title: Embedded Systems 101: Beginner's Guide
description:
The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from Embedded Systems that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

Welcome to one of the most genuinely useful events Photography Club has run this academic year. We know that phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let us be specific about what we mean. This session on Embedded Systems was designed in response to direct feedback from students who sat placement interviews, bombed questions they had never been exposed to, and came back asking us to do something about it. We listened. What you will see today is the result of six weeks of curriculum design, two rounds of feedback from working engineers, and one very honest conversation about what actually matters.

A few things we want to be transparent about. The facilitators running this session are not perfect. They will make mistakes in live demonstrations. When that happens, we will debug together, which is arguably the most educational part of any session. Photography Club believes in showing real work, not curated performances. If that sounds like a good use of your Saturday afternoon, we think you will find this event genuinely worthwhile.

After the event, all registered attendees will receive a curated resource pack: three links our facilitators actually use, two books they would recommend if pressed, and one honest assessment of the gaps in their own knowledge of Embedded Systems and how they are addressing them. We include the last one because we think intellectual honesty about what you do not know is as valuable as knowledge itself, and we want to model that for students.

Seats will run out before the deadline does. Register now.

title: Panel Discussion: React & Next.js
description:
A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with React & Next.js professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. But if you are hoping for a deep technical dive at the cutting edge of the field, this is not that event. We are going for breadth and confidence-building, not depth. The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

Here is what the session actually looks like. We open with a fifteen-minute orientation that covers the landscape of React & Next.js — where it sits relative to everything else you have learned, why it matters now more than it did five years ago, and what a working professional actually does with it on a Monday morning. This part is deliberately fast. We do not want to spend half the session on theory that you could have absorbed from a Wikipedia article. We want to get to the part where you do things.

The idea for this event on React & Next.js came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

The speakers for this event have been chosen for one reason above all others: they can explain things clearly. It sounds obvious, but it is surprisingly rare. We have had sessions in the past where technically brilliant people presented information in a way that left the room more confused than when they arrived. We learnt from that. The facilitators you will hear from today have been tested in smaller settings first, given feedback, and iterated. What you are getting is a refined version, not a first draft.

Seats will run out before the deadline does. Register now.

title: Annual Open Source Contribution Competition
description:

title: Networking Night: Game Development
description:
The idea for this event on Game Development came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for Game Development — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

A few things we want to be transparent about. The facilitators running this session are not perfect. They will make mistakes in live demonstrations. When that happens, we will debug together, which is arguably the most educational part of any session. Robotics Club believes in showing real work, not curated performances. If that sounds like a good use of your Saturday afternoon, we think you will find this event genuinely worthwhile.

Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where Game Development was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with Game Development. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together.

After the event, all registered attendees will receive a curated resource pack: three links our facilitators actually use, two books they would recommend if pressed, and one honest assessment of the gaps in their own knowledge of Game Development and how they are addressing them. We include the last one because we think intellectual honesty about what you do not know is as valuable as knowledge itself, and we want to model that for students.

The event is free. The knowledge is permanent. The registration takes thirty seconds. There is no reason not to.

title: Robotics & Automation Sprint
description:
We want to be upfront about what this event is not. It is not a placement coaching session. It is not a certificate farm. It is not a box to tick on your co-curricular activity sheet. It is a room full of people who are genuinely curious about Robotics & Automation, facilitated by people who have invested real time in understanding it, with the goal of leaving everyone slightly less confused than they arrived. If that sounds like a good way to spend a few hours, the door is open.

We have structured this event around a principle that Music Society cares about deeply: learning by producing, not learning by consuming. Every segment of this session on Robotics & Automation includes a moment where you must make something — a diagram, a line of code, a decision, a prediction. These are not graded. They will not be collected. They are for you, because the act of producing forces your brain to process information in a way that passive watching simply does not.

Most events on Robotics & Automation are designed for people who already have a foundation and just want to go deeper. This one is different. Music Society built this session specifically for the student who has heard the term a hundred times, nodded along in class, and quietly panicked when asked to actually do something with it. You are the target audience. There is no shame in being here at the beginning — there is only the question of what you choose to do about it. This is your practical starting point.

The person leading today's session on Robotics & Automation was not our first choice — they were our third. Our first two choices were excellent but unavailable on this date. Our third choice turned out to be better than either of the first two, which is a useful reminder that the best facilitators are not always the most obvious ones. They bring a perspective on Robotics & Automation that we had not fully anticipated when we reached out, and we think it makes the session richer for it.

Food and drinks will be available throughout. We mention this not to bribe you into attending — the content should do that — but because we have noticed that sessions run better when people are not hungry. Please eat something before you arrive as well. A three-hour session on Robotics & Automation on an empty stomach is not the optimal learning environment, and we speak from experience.

Seats will run out before the deadline does. Register now.

title: Seminar on Blockchain
description:
Here is what the session actually looks like. We open with a fifteen-minute orientation that covers the landscape of Blockchain — where it sits relative to everything else you have learned, why it matters now more than it did five years ago, and what a working professional actually does with it on a Monday morning. This part is deliberately fast. We do not want to spend half the session on theory that you could have absorbed from a Wikipedia article. We want to get to the part where you do things.

Most events on Blockchain are designed for people who already have a foundation and just want to go deeper. This one is different. IEEE Student Branch built this session specifically for the student who has heard the term a hundred times, nodded along in class, and quietly panicked when asked to actually do something with it. You are the target audience. There is no shame in being here at the beginning — there is only the question of what you choose to do about it. This is your practical starting point.

We want to be upfront about what this event is not. It is not a placement coaching session. It is not a certificate farm. It is not a box to tick on your co-curricular activity sheet. It is a room full of people who are genuinely curious about Blockchain, facilitated by people who have invested real time in understanding it, with the goal of leaving everyone slightly less confused than they arrived. If that sounds like a good way to spend a few hours, the door is open.

We will see you there. Bring your laptop, bring your questions, and bring someone who needs this as much as you do.

title: System Design Bootcamp
description:
There is a version of this event that would have been easy to run — a polished slide deck, a speaker talking at you for ninety minutes, a group photo at the end. We chose not to do that version. Instead, the Drama Club spent the last month building a session on System Design that puts you in the driver's seat from the first minute. The facilitators are here as guides, not lecturers. The agenda is a suggestion, not a script. And the only metric we care about at the end is whether you leave more capable than when you arrived.

The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from System Design that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with System Design professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. But if you are hoping for a deep technical dive at the cutting edge of the field, this is not that event. We are going for breadth and confidence-building, not depth. The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

We considered bringing in an external speaker for this one and decided against it. The best person to talk to RVCE students about navigating System Design in the current environment is someone who was an RVCE student recently enough to remember what it felt like — and senior enough to have perspective on it. That is what we have. Someone who has been where you are, done what you are trying to do, and is willing to be honest about how they actually got there.

After the event, all registered attendees will receive a curated resource pack: three links our facilitators actually use, two books they would recommend if pressed, and one honest assessment of the gaps in their own knowledge of System Design and how they are addressing them. We include the last one because we think intellectual honesty about what you do not know is as valuable as knowledge itself, and we want to model that for students.

Show up. Work hard. Leave better. That is all we ask.

title: REST APIs — Guest Lecture
description:

A few things we want to be transparent about. The facilitators running this session are not perfect. They will make mistakes in live demonstrations. When that happens, we will debug together, which is arguably the most educational part of any session. Robotics Club believes in showing real work, not curated performances. If that sounds like a good use of your Saturday afternoon, we think you will find this event genuinely worthwhile.

Food and drinks will be available throughout. We mention this not to bribe you into attending — the content should do that — but because we have noticed that sessions run better when people are not hungry. Please eat something before you arrive as well. A three-hour session on REST APIs on an empty stomach is not the optimal learning environment, and we speak from experience.

Show up. Work hard. Leave better. That is all we ask.

title: Career Fair: System Design
description:
A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with System Design professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. The idea for this event on System Design came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

Here is what the session actually looks like. We open with a fifteen-minute orientation that covers the landscape of System Design — where it sits relative to everything else you have learned, why it matters now more than it did five years ago, and what a working professional actually does with it on a Monday morning. This part is deliberately fast. We do not want to spend half the session on theory that you could have absorbed from a Wikipedia article. We want to get to the part where you do things.

Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where System Design was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with System Design. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together.

Certificates of participation will be issued to everyone who attends. We know that is a secondary concern for most people in this room, and we are glad for that. But for those who need it — for internship applications, for placement interviews, for anxious parents — it exists and it will arrive in your inbox within 48 hours of the event's close. Please register with your college email address to ensure delivery.

The event is free. The knowledge is permanent. The registration takes thirty seconds. There is no reason not to.

title: Open Mic: Research Methodology
description:
One thing that consistently surprises attendees at Coding Club RVCE events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on Research Methodology — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. They are a core part of what we are trying to create.

There is a version of this event that would have been easy to run — a polished slide deck, a speaker talking at you for ninety minutes, a group photo at the end. We chose not to do that version. Instead, the Coding Club RVCE spent the last month building a session on Research Methodology that puts you in the driver's seat from the first minute. The facilitators are here as guides, not lecturers. The agenda is a suggestion, not a script. And the only metric we care about at the end is whether you leave more capable than when you arrived.

We have structured this event around a principle that Coding Club RVCE cares about deeply: learning by producing, not learning by consuming. Every segment of this session on Research Methodology includes a moment where you must make something — a diagram, a line of code, a decision, a prediction. These are not graded. They will not be collected. They are for you, because the act of producing forces your brain to process information in a way that passive watching simply does not.

Food and drinks will be available throughout. We mention this not to bribe you into attending — the content should do that — but because we have noticed that sessions run better when people are not hungry. Please eat something before you arrive as well. A three-hour session on Research Methodology on an empty stomach is not the optimal learning environment, and we speak from experience.

We will see you there. Bring your laptop, bring your questions, and bring someone who needs this as much as you do.

title: Open Mic: Cloud Computing
description:
We want to be upfront about what this event is not. It is not a placement coaching session. It is not a certificate farm. It is not a box to tick on your co-curricular activity sheet. It is a room full of people who are genuinely curious about Cloud Computing, facilitated by people who have invested real time in understanding it, with the goal of leaving everyone slightly less confused than they arrived. If that sounds like a good way to spend a few hours, the door is open.

We have structured this event around a principle that Music Society cares about deeply: learning by producing, not learning by consuming. Every segment of this session on Cloud Computing includes a moment where you must make something — a diagram, a line of code, a decision, a prediction. These are not graded. They will not be collected. They are for you, because the act of producing forces your brain to process information in a way that passive watching simply does not.

The idea for this event on Cloud Computing came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where Cloud Computing was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with Cloud Computing. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together.

Show up. Work hard. Leave better. That is all we ask.

title: Career Prep & Placement Showcase
description:
A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with Career Prep & Placement professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. But if you are hoping for a deep technical dive at the cutting edge of the field, this is not that event. We are going for breadth and confidence-building, not depth. The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

Welcome to one of the most genuinely useful events Design Guild has run this academic year. We know that phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let us be specific about what we mean. This session on Career Prep & Placement was designed in response to direct feedback from students who sat placement interviews, bombed questions they had never been exposed to, and came back asking us to do something about it. We listened. What you will see today is the result of six weeks of curriculum design, two rounds of feedback from working engineers, and one very honest conversation about what actually matters.

The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for Career Prep & Placement — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

We considered bringing in an external speaker for this one and decided against it. The best person to talk to RVCE students about navigating Career Prep & Placement in the current environment is someone who was an RVCE student recently enough to remember what it felt like — and senior enough to have perspective on it. That is what we have. Someone who has been where you are, done what you are trying to do, and is willing to be honest about how they actually got there.

The event is free. The knowledge is permanent. The registration takes thirty seconds. There is no reason not to.

title: Panel Discussion: System Design
description:
We want to be upfront about what this event is not. It is not a placement coaching session. It is not a certificate farm. It is not a box to tick on your co-curricular activity sheet. It is a room full of people who are genuinely curious about System Design, facilitated by people who have invested real time in understanding it, with the goal of leaving everyone slightly less confused than they arrived. If that sounds like a good way to spend a few hours, the door is open.

The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from System Design that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

There is a version of this event that would have been easy to run — a polished slide deck, a speaker talking at you for ninety minutes, a group photo at the end. We chose not to do that version. Instead, the Quizzing Club spent the last month building a session on System Design that puts you in the driver's seat from the first minute. The facilitators are here as guides, not lecturers. The agenda is a suggestion, not a script. And the only metric we care about at the end is whether you leave more capable than when you arrived.

We considered bringing in an external speaker for this one and decided against it. The best person to talk to RVCE students about navigating System Design in the current environment is someone who was an RVCE student recently enough to remember what it felt like — and senior enough to have perspective on it. That is what we have. Someone who has been where you are, done what you are trying to do, and is willing to be honest about how they actually got there.

After the event, all registered attendees will receive a curated resource pack: three links our facilitators actually use, two books they would recommend if pressed, and one honest assessment of the gaps in their own knowledge of System Design and how they are addressing them. We include the last one because we think intellectual honesty about what you do not know is as valuable as knowledge itself, and we want to model that for students.

Seats will run out before the deadline does. Register now.

description:
A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with Finance 101 professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. But if you are hoping for a deep technical dive at the cutting edge of the field, this is not that event. We are going for breadth and confidence-building, not depth. The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

Welcome to one of the most genuinely useful events Drama Club has run this academic year. We know that phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let us be specific about what we mean. This session on Finance 101 was designed in response to direct feedback from students who sat placement interviews, bombed questions they had never been exposed to, and came back asking us to do something about it. We listened. What you will see today is the result of six weeks of curriculum design, two rounds of feedback from working engineers, and one very honest conversation about what actually matters.

We have structured this event around a principle that Drama Club cares about deeply: learning by producing, not learning by consuming. Every segment of this session on Finance 101 includes a moment where you must make something — a diagram, a line of code, a decision, a prediction. These are not graded. They will not be collected. They are for you, because the act of producing forces your brain to process information in a way that passive watching simply does not.

Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where Finance 101 was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with Finance 101. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together.

Certificates of participation will be issued to everyone who attends. We know that is a secondary concern for most people in this room, and we are glad for that. description:

The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

Most events on Data Structures are designed for people who already have a foundation and just want to go deeper. This one is different. Entrepreneurship Cell built this session specifically for the student who has heard the term a hundred times, nodded along in class, and quietly panicked when asked to actually do something with it. You are the target audience. There is no shame in being here at the beginning — there is only the question of what you choose to do about it. This is your practical starting point.

The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from Data Structures that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

The speakers for this event have been chosen for one reason above all others: they can explain things clearly. It sounds obvious, but it is surprisingly rare. We have had sessions in the past where technically brilliant people presented information in a way that left the room more confused than when they arrived. We learnt from that. The facilitators you will hear from today have been tested in smaller settings first, given feedback, and iterated. What you are getting is a refined version, not a first draft.

If you have read this far and you are still not registered, we genuinely want to know what is stopping you. DM us on Instagram.

title: Networking Night: React & Next.js
description:
The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for React & Next.js — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

Most events on React & Next.js are designed for people who already have a foundation and just want to go deeper. This one is different. Entrepreneurship Cell built this session specifically for the student who has heard the term a hundred times, nodded along in class, and quietly panicked when asked to actually do something with it. You are the target audience. There is no shame in being here at the beginning — there is only the question of what you choose to do about it. This is your practical starting point.

A few things we want to be transparent about. The facilitators running this session are not perfect. They will make mistakes in live demonstrations. When that happens, we will debug together, which is arguably the most educational part of any session. Entrepreneurship Cell believes in showing real work, not curated performances. If that sounds like a good use of your Saturday afternoon, we think you will find this event genuinely worthwhile.

Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where React & Next.js was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with React & Next.js. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together.

We will see you there. Bring your laptop, bring your questions, and bring someone who needs this as much as you do.

title: Panel Discussion: Entrepreneurship

title: Hands-on Robotics & Automation Session

The idea for this event on Robotics & Automation came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

We want to be upfront about what this event is not. It is not a placement coaching session. It is not a certificate farm. It is not a box to tick on your co-curricular activity sheet. It is a room full of people who are genuinely curious about Robotics & Automation, facilitated by people who have invested real time in understanding it, with the goal of leaving everyone slightly less confused than they arrived. If that sounds like a good way to spend a few hours, the door is open.

The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for Robotics & Automation — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where Robotics & Automation was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with Robotics & Automation. title: Industry Talk: Data Structures
description:
The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for Data Structures — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with Data Structures professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

Most events on Data Structures are designed for people who already have a foundation and just want to go deeper. This one is different. Sports Council built this session specifically for the student who has heard the term a hundred times, nodded along in class, and quietly panicked when asked to actually do something with it. You are the target audience. There is no shame in being here at the beginning — there is only the question of what you choose to do about it. This is your practical starting point.

After the event, all registered attendees will receive a curated resource pack: three links our facilitators actually use, two books they would recommend if pressed, and one honest assessment of the gaps in their own knowledge of Data Structures and how they are addressing them. We include the last one because we think intellectual honesty about what you do not know is as valuable as knowledge itself, and we want to model that for students.

This is Sports Council's commitment: if you attend and feel it was not worth your time, tell us directly. We will listen and we will fix it for next time. That is how we have gotten better every semester.

A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with Cloud Computing professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. But if you are hoping for a deep technical dive at the cutting edge of the field, this is not that event. We are going for breadth and confidence-building, not depth. The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

There is a version of this event that would have been easy to run — a polished slide deck, a speaker talking at you for ninety minutes, a group photo at the end. We chose not to do that version. Instead, the AI & ML Club spent the last month building a session on Cloud Computing that puts you in the driver's seat from the first minute. The facilitators are here as guides, not lecturers. The agenda is a suggestion, not a script. And the only metric we care about at the end is whether you leave more capable than when you arrived.

The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from Cloud Computing that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

The speakers for this event have been chosen for one reason above all others: they can explain things clearly. It sounds obvious, but it is surprisingly rare. We have had sessions in the past where technically brilliant people presented information in a way that left the room more confused than when they arrived. We learnt from that. The facilitators you will hear from today have been tested in smaller settings first, given feedback, and iterated. What you are getting is a refined version, not a first draft.

Certificates of participation will be issued to everyone who attends. We know that is a secondary concern for most people in this room, and we are glad for that. But for those who need it — for internship applications, for placement interviews, for anxious parents — it exists and it will arrive in your inbox within 48 hours of the event's close. Please register with your college email address to ensure delivery.

The event is free. The knowledge is permanent. The registration takes thirty seconds. There is no reason not to.

title: Seminar on Cloud Computing
description:
Welcome to one of the most genuinely useful events Coding Club RVCE has run this academic year. We know that phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let us be specific about what we mean. This session on Cloud Computing was designed in response to direct feedback from students who sat placement interviews, bombed questions they had never been exposed to, and came back asking us to do something about it. We listened. What you will see today is the result of six weeks of curriculum design, two rounds of feedback from working engineers, and one very honest conversation about what actually matters.

One thing that consistently surprises attendees at Coding Club RVCE events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on Cloud Computing — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. They are a core part of what we are trying to create.

Here is what the session actually looks like. We open with a fifteen-minute orientation that covers the landscape of Cloud Computing — where it sits relative to everything else you have learned, why it matters now more than it did five years ago, and what a working professional actually does with it on a Monday morning. This part is deliberately fast. We do not want to spend half the session on theory that you could have absorbed from a Wikipedia article. We want to get to the part where you do things.

Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where Cloud Computing was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with Cloud Computing. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together.

The venue has been chosen specifically for its layout. We needed a room where the facilitator could move around freely, where breakout discussions could happen without disrupting the main session, and where the acoustics would not turn every explanation into an echo. We did a walkthrough last week. The space works. If you have attended events at other venues and found them frustrating for these reasons, this one should be different.

Registration is open now. Space is limited. If you are on the fence, the fence is the wrong place to be.

title: Embedded Systems Sprint
description:
We want to be upfront about what this event is not. It is not a placement coaching session. It is not a certificate farm. It is not a box to tick on your co-curricular activity sheet. It is a room full of people who are genuinely curious about Embedded Systems, facilitated by people who have invested real time in understanding it, with the goal of leaving everyone slightly less confused than they arrived. If that sounds like a good way to spend a few hours, the door is open.

The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for Embedded Systems — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

Most events on Embedded Systems are designed for people who already have a foundation and just want to go deeper. This one is different. Finance Club built this session specifically for the student who has heard the term a hundred times, nodded along in class, and quietly panicked when asked to actually do something with it. You are the target audience. There is no shame in being here at the beginning — there is only the question of what you choose to do about it. This is your practical starting point.

Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where Embedded Systems was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with Embedded Systems. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together.

The event is free. The knowledge is permanent. The registration takes thirty seconds. There is no reason not to.

title: Sustainable Tech — Guest Lecture
description:
Here is what the session actually looks like. We open with a fifteen-minute orientation that covers the landscape of Sustainable Tech — where it sits relative to everything else you have learned, why it matters now more than it did five years ago, and what a working professional actually does with it on a Monday morning. This part is deliberately fast. We do not want to spend half the session on theory that you could have absorbed from a Wikipedia article. We want to get to the part where you do things.

A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with Sustainable Tech professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. But if you are hoping for a deep technical dive at the cutting edge of the field, this is not that event. We are going for breadth and confidence-building, not depth. The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

The idea for this event on Sustainable Tech came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

After the event, all registered attendees will receive a curated resource pack: three links our facilitators actually use, two books they would recommend if pressed, and one honest assessment of the gaps in their own knowledge of Sustainable Tech and how they are addressing them. We include the last one because we think intellectual honesty about what you do not know is as valuable as knowledge itself, and we want to model that for students.

Seats will run out before the deadline does. Register now.

title: Panel Discussion: Career Prep & Placement
description:
The idea for this event on Career Prep & Placement came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

We have structured this event around a principle that Open Source Club cares about deeply: learning by producing, not learning by consuming. Every segment of this session on Career Prep & Placement includes a moment where you must make something — a diagram, a line of code, a decision, a prediction. These are not graded. They will not be collected. They are for you, because the act of producing forces your brain to process information in a way that passive watching simply does not.

A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with Career Prep & Placement professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. But if you are hoping for a deep technical dive at the cutting edge of the field, this is not that event. We are going for breadth and confidence-building, not depth. The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

The person leading today's session on Career Prep & Placement was not our first choice — they were our third. Our first two choices were excellent but unavailable on this date. Our third choice turned out to be better than either of the first two, which is a useful reminder that the best facilitators are not always the most obvious ones. They bring a perspective on Career Prep & Placement that we had not fully anticipated when we reached out, and we think it makes the session richer for it.

The venue has been chosen specifically for its layout. We needed a room where the facilitator could move around freely, where breakout discussions could happen without disrupting the main session, and where the acoustics would not turn every explanation into an echo. We did a walkthrough last week. The space works. If you have attended events at other venues and found them frustrating for these reasons, this one should be different.

If you have read this far and you are still not registered, we genuinely want to know what is stopping you. DM us on Instagram.

title: Seminar on Research Methodology
description:
The idea for this event on Research Methodology came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from Research Methodology that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

We want to be upfront about what this event is not. It is not a placement coaching session. It is not a certificate farm. It is not a box to tick on your co-curricular activity sheet. It is a room full of people who are genuinely curious about Research Methodology, facilitated by people who have invested real time in understanding it, with the goal of leaving everyone slightly less confused than they arrived. If that sounds like a good way to spend a few hours, the door is open.

We considered bringing in an external speaker for this one and decided against it. The best person to talk to RVCE students about navigating Research Methodology in the current environment is someone who was an RVCE student recently enough to remember what it felt like — and senior enough to have perspective on it. That is what we have. Someone who has been where you are, done what you are trying to do, and is willing to be honest about how they actually got there.

The venue has been chosen specifically for its layout. We needed a room where the facilitator could move around freely, where breakout discussions could happen without disrupting the main session, and where the acoustics would not turn every explanation into an echo. We did a walkthrough last week. The space works. If you have attended events at other venues and found them frustrating for these reasons, this one should be different.

Show up. Work hard. Leave better. That is all we ask.

title: Embedded Systems 101: Beginner's Guide
description:
We have structured this event around a principle that Debate Society cares about deeply: learning by producing, not learning by consuming. Every segment of this session on Embedded Systems includes a moment where you must make something — a diagram, a line of code, a decision, a prediction. These are not graded. They will not be collected. They are for you, because the act of producing forces your brain to process information in a way that passive watching simply does not.

There is a version of this event that would have been easy to run — a polished slide deck, a speaker talking at you for ninety minutes, a group photo at the end. We chose not to do that version. Instead, the Debate Society spent the last month building a session on Embedded Systems that puts you in the driver's seat from the first minute. The facilitators are here as guides, not lecturers. The agenda is a suggestion, not a script. And the only metric we care about at the end is whether you leave more capable than when you arrived.

One thing that consistently surprises attendees at Debate Society events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on Embedded Systems — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. They are a core part of what we are trying to create.

The person leading today's session on Embedded Systems was not our first choice — they were our third. Our first two choices were excellent but unavailable on this date. Our third choice turned out to be better than either of the first two, which is a useful reminder that the best facilitators are not always the most obvious ones. They bring a perspective on Embedded Systems that we had not fully anticipated when we reached out, and we think it makes the session richer for it.

Certificates of participation will be issued to everyone who attends. We know that is a secondary concern for most people in this room, and we are glad for that. But for those who need it — for internship applications, for placement interviews, for anxious parents — it exists and it will arrive in your inbox within 48 hours of the event's close. Please register with your college email address to ensure delivery.

Registration is open now. Space is limited. If you are on the fence, the fence is the wrong place to be.

title: Finance 101 Hackathon
description:
Welcome to one of the most genuinely useful events IEEE Student Branch has run this academic year. We know that phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let us be specific about what we mean. This session on Finance 101 was designed in response to direct feedback from students who sat placement interviews, bombed questions they had never been exposed to, and came back asking us to do something about it. We listened. What you will see today is the result of six weeks of curriculum design, two rounds of feedback from working engineers, and one very honest conversation about what actually matters.

A few things we want to be transparent about. The facilitators running this session are not perfect. They will make mistakes in live demonstrations. When that happens, we will debug together, which is arguably the most educational part of any session. IEEE Student Branch believes in showing real work, not curated performances. If that sounds like a good use of your Saturday afternoon, we think you will find this event genuinely worthwhile.

The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for Finance 101 — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

The speakers for this event have been chosen for one reason above all others: they can explain things clearly. It sounds obvious, but it is surprisingly rare. We have had sessions in the past where technically brilliant people presented information in a way that left the room more confused than when they arrived. We learnt from that. The facilitators you will hear from today have been tested in smaller settings first, given feedback, and iterated. What you are getting is a refined version, not a first draft.

If you have read this far and you are still not registered, we genuinely want to know what is stopping you. DM us on Instagram.

title: Research Methodology Hackathon
description:

We have structured this event around a principle that Coding Club RVCE cares about deeply: learning by producing, not learning by consuming. Every segment of this session on Research Methodology includes a moment where you must make something — a diagram, a line of code, a decision, a prediction. These are not graded. They will not be collected. They are for you, because the act of producing forces your brain to process information in a way that passive watching simply does not.

There is a version of this event that would have been easy to run — a polished slide deck, a speaker talking at you for ninety minutes, a group photo at the end. We chose not to do that version. Instead, the Coding Club RVCE spent the last month building a session on Research Methodology that puts you in the driver's seat from the first minute. The facilitators are here as guides, not lecturers. The agenda is a suggestion, not a script. And the only metric we care about at the end is whether you leave more capable than when you arrived.

The person leading today's session on Research Methodology was not our first choice — they were our third. Our first two choices were excellent but unavailable on this date. Our third choice turned out to be better than either of the first two, which is a useful reminder that the best facilitators are not always the most obvious ones. description:

We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on Machine Learning — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. Most events on Machine Learning are designed for people who already have a foundation and just want to go deeper. This one is different. Photography Club built this session specifically for the student who has heard the term a hundred times, nodded along in class, and quietly panicked when asked to actually do something with it. You are the target audience. There is no shame in being here at the beginning — there is only the question of what you choose to do about it. This is your practical starting point.

This is Photography Club's commitment: if you attend and feel it was not worth your time, tell us directly. We will listen and we will fix it for next time. That is how we have gotten better every semester.

title: Open Source Contribution Sprint
description:
One thing that consistently surprises attendees at Open Source Club events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on Open Source Contribution — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. They are a core part of what we are trying to create.

We have structured this event around a principle that Open Source Club cares about deeply: learning by producing, not learning by consuming. Every segment of this session on Open Source Contribution includes a moment where you must make something — a diagram, a line of code, a decision, a prediction. These are not graded. They will not be collected. They are for you, because the act of producing forces your brain to process information in a way that passive watching simply does not.

The idea for this event on Open Source Contribution came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where Open Source Contribution was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with Open Source Contribution. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together.

After the event, all registered attendees will receive a curated resource pack: three links our facilitators actually use, two books they would recommend if pressed, and one honest assessment of the gaps in their own knowledge of Open Source Contribution and how they are addressing them. We include the last one because we think intellectual honesty about what you do not know is as valuable as knowledge itself, and we want to model that for students.

Registration is open now. Space is limited. If you are on the fence, the fence is the wrong place to be.

title: Open Mic: Embedded Systems
description:
The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for Embedded Systems — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

There is a version of this event that would have been easy to run — a polished slide deck, a speaker talking at you for ninety minutes, a group photo at the end. We chose not to do that version. Instead, the Sports Council spent the last month building a session on Embedded Systems that puts you in the driver's seat from the first minute. The facilitators are here as guides, not lecturers. The agenda is a suggestion, not a script. And the only metric we care about at the end is whether you leave more capable than when you arrived.

A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with Embedded Systems professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. But if you are hoping for a deep technical dive at the cutting edge of the field, this is not that event. We are going for breadth and confidence-building, not depth. The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

We considered bringing in an external speaker for this one and decided against it. The best person to talk to RVCE students about navigating Embedded Systems in the current environment is someone who was an RVCE student recently enough to remember what it felt like — and senior enough to have perspective on it. That is what we have. Someone who has been where you are, done what you are trying to do, and is willing to be honest about how they actually got there.

Certificates of participation will be issued to everyone who attends. We know that is a secondary concern for most people in this room, and we are glad for that. But for those who need it — for internship applications, for placement interviews, for anxious parents — it exists and it will arrive in your inbox within 48 hours of the event's close. Please register with your college email address to ensure delivery.

If you have read this far and you are still not registered, we genuinely want to know what is stopping you. DM us on Instagram.
