title: Networking Night: Blockchain
description:
The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from Blockchain that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

One thing that consistently surprises attendees at Debate Society events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on Blockchain — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. They are a core part of what we are trying to create.

There is a version of this event that would have been easy to run — a polished slide deck, a speaker talking at you for ninety minutes, a group photo at the end. We chose not to do that version. Instead, the Debate Society spent the last month building a session on Blockchain that puts you in the driver's seat from the first minute. The facilitators are here as guides, not lecturers. The agenda is a suggestion, not a script. And the only metric we care about at the end is whether you leave more capable than when you arrived.

We will see you there. Bring your laptop, bring your questions, and bring someone who needs this as much as you do.

title: Robotics & Automation 101: Beginner's Guide
description:
Most events on Robotics & Automation are designed for people who already have a foundation and just want to go deeper. This one is different. Robotics Club built this session specifically for the student who has heard the term a hundred times, nodded along in class, and quietly panicked when asked to actually do something with it. You are the target audience. There is no shame in being here at the beginning — there is only the question of what you choose to do about it. This is your practical starting point.

Here is what the session actually looks like. We open with a fifteen-minute orientation that covers the landscape of Robotics & Automation — where it sits relative to everything else you have learned, why it matters now more than it did five years ago, and what a working professional actually does with it on a Monday morning. This part is deliberately fast. We do not want to spend half the session on theory that you could have absorbed from a Wikipedia article. We want to get to the part where you do things.

A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with Robotics & Automation professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. But if you are hoping for a deep technical dive at the cutting edge of the field, this is not that event. We are going for breadth and confidence-building, not depth. The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

We considered bringing in an external speaker for this one and decided against it. The best person to talk to RVCE students about navigating Robotics & Automation in the current environment is someone who was an RVCE student recently enough to remember what it felt like — and senior enough to have perspective on it. That is what we have. Someone who has been where you are, done what you are trying to do, and is willing to be honest about how they actually got there.

Food and drinks will be available throughout. We mention this not to bribe you into attending — the content should do that — but because we have noticed that sessions run better when people are not hungry. Please eat something before you arrive as well. A three-hour session on Robotics & Automation on an empty stomach is not the optimal learning environment, and we speak from experience.

We will see you there. Bring your laptop, bring your questions, and bring someone who needs this as much as you do.

A few things we want to be transparent about. The facilitators running this session are not perfect. They will make mistakes in live demonstrations. When that happens, we will debug together, which is arguably the most educational part of any session. Debate Society believes in showing real work, not curated performances. If that sounds like a good use of your Saturday afternoon, we think you will find this event genuinely worthwhile.

There is a version of this event that would have been easy to run — a polished slide deck, a speaker talking at you for ninety minutes, a group photo at the end. We chose not to do that version. Instead, the Debate Society spent the last month building a session on Blockchain that puts you in the driver's seat from the first minute. The facilitators are here as guides, not lecturers. The agenda is a suggestion, not a script. And the only metric we care about at the end is whether you leave more capable than when you arrived.

Here is what the session actually looks like. We open with a fifteen-minute orientation that covers the landscape of Blockchain — where it sits relative to everything else you have learned, why it matters now more than it did five years ago, and what a working professional actually does with it on a Monday morning. This part is deliberately fast. We do not want to spend half the session on theory that you could have absorbed from a Wikipedia article. We want to get to the part where you do things.

Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where Blockchain was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with Blockchain. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together.

Certificates of participation will be issued to everyone who attends. We know that is a secondary concern for most people in this room, and we are glad for that. But for those who need it — for internship applications, for placement interviews, for anxious parents — it exists and it will arrive in your inbox within 48 hours of the event's close. Please register with your college email address to ensure delivery.

Seats will run out before the deadline does. Register now.

title: Industry Talk: IoT Projects
description:
A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with IoT Projects professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. But if you are hoping for a deep technical dive at the cutting edge of the field, this is not that event. We are going for breadth and confidence-building, not depth. The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from IoT Projects that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

Most events on IoT Projects are designed for people who already have a foundation and just want to go deeper. This one is different. Robotics Club built this session specifically for the student who has heard the term a hundred times, nodded along in class, and quietly panicked when asked to actually do something with it. You are the target audience. There is no shame in being here at the beginning — there is only the question of what you choose to do about it. This is your practical starting point.

The speakers for this event have been chosen for one reason above all others: they can explain things clearly. It sounds obvious, but it is surprisingly rare. We have had sessions in the past where technically brilliant people presented information in a way that left the room more confused than when they arrived. We learnt from that. The facilitators you will hear from today have been tested in smaller settings first, given feedback, and iterated. What you are getting is a refined version, not a first draft.

The venue has been chosen specifically for its layout. We needed a room where the facilitator could move around freely, where breakout discussions could happen without disrupting the main session, and where the acoustics would not turn every explanation into an echo. We did a walkthrough last week. The space works. If you have attended events at other venues and found them frustrating for these reasons, this one should be different.

If you have read this far and you are still not registered, we genuinely want to know what is stopping you. DM us on Instagram.

title: System Design Showcase
description:
We have structured this event around a principle that Entrepreneurship Cell cares about deeply: learning by producing, not learning by consuming. Every segment of this session on System Design includes a moment where you must make something — a diagram, a line of code, a decision, a prediction. These are not graded. They will not be collected. They are for you, because the act of producing forces your brain to process information in a way that passive watching simply does not.

The idea for this event on System Design came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

One thing that consistently surprises attendees at Entrepreneurship Cell events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on System Design — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. They are a core part of what we are trying to create.

Food and drinks will be available throughout. We mention this not to bribe you into attending — the content should do that — but because we have noticed that sessions run better when people are not hungry. Please eat something before you arrive as well. A three-hour session on System Design on an empty stomach is not the optimal learning environment, and we speak from experience.

Show up. Work hard. Leave better. That is all we ask.

There is a version of this event that would have been easy to run — a polished slide deck, a speaker talking at you for ninety minutes, a group photo at the end. We chose not to do that version. Instead, the Photography Club spent the last month building a session on AR/VR Development that puts you in the driver's seat from the first minute. The facilitators are here as guides, not lecturers. The agenda is a suggestion, not a script. And the only metric we care about at the end is whether you leave more capable than when you arrived.

We have structured this event around a principle that Photography Club cares about deeply: learning by producing, not learning by consuming. Every segment of this session on AR/VR Development includes a moment where you must make something — a diagram, a line of code, a decision, a prediction. These are not graded. They will not be collected. They are for you, because the act of producing forces your brain to process information in a way that passive watching simply does not.

A few things we want to be transparent about. The facilitators running this session are not perfect. They will make mistakes in live demonstrations. When that happens, we will debug together, which is arguably the most educational part of any session. Photography Club believes in showing real work, not curated performances. If that sounds like a good use of your Saturday afternoon, we think you will find this event genuinely worthwhile.

Seats will run out before the deadline does. Register now.

title: Seminar on Finance 101
description:
A few things we want to be transparent about. The facilitators running this session are not perfect. They will make mistakes in live demonstrations. Welcome to one of the most genuinely useful events Robotics Club has run this academic year. We know that phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let us be specific about what we mean. This session on Finance 101 was designed in response to direct feedback from students who sat placement interviews, bombed questions they had never been exposed to, and came back asking us to do something about it. We listened. What you will see today is the result of six weeks of curriculum design, two rounds of feedback from working engineers, and one very honest conversation about what actually matters.

Here is what the session actually looks like. We open with a fifteen-minute orientation that covers the landscape of Finance 101 — where it sits relative to everything else you have learned, why it matters now more than it did five years ago, and what a working professional actually does with it on a Monday morning. This part is deliberately fast. We do not want to spend half the session on theory that you could have absorbed from a Wikipedia article. We want to get to the part where you do things.

We will see you there. Bring your laptop, bring your questions, and bring someone who needs this as much as you do.

title: Blockchain Showcase
description:
Most events on Blockchain are designed for people who already have a foundation and just want to go deeper. This one is different. Literary Club built this session specifically for the student who has heard the term a hundred times, nodded along in class, and quietly panicked when asked to actually do something with it. You are the target audience. There is no shame in being here at the beginning — there is only the question of what you choose to do about it. This is your practical starting point.

The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for Blockchain — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

One thing that consistently surprises attendees at Literary Club events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on Blockchain — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. They are a core part of what we are trying to create.

We considered bringing in an external speaker for this one and decided against it. The best person to talk to RVCE students about navigating Blockchain in the current environment is someone who was an RVCE student recently enough to remember what it felt like — and senior enough to have perspective on it. That is what we have. Someone who has been where you are, done what you are trying to do, and is willing to be honest about how they actually got there.

Registration is open now. Space is limited. If you are on the fence, the fence is the wrong place to be.

title: Hands-on Competitive Programming Session
description:
We want to be upfront about what this event is not. It is not a placement coaching session. It is not a certificate farm. It is not a box to tick on your co-curricular activity sheet. It is a room full of people who are genuinely curious about Competitive Programming, facilitated by people who have invested real time in understanding it, with the goal of leaving everyone slightly less confused than they arrived. If that sounds like a good way to spend a few hours, the door is open.

The idea for this event on Competitive Programming came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from Competitive Programming that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

We considered bringing in an external speaker for this one and decided against it. The best person to talk to RVCE students about navigating Competitive Programming in the current environment is someone who was an RVCE student recently enough to remember what it felt like — and senior enough to have perspective on it. That is what we have. Someone who has been where you are, done what you are trying to do, and is willing to be honest about how they actually got there.

After the event, all registered attendees will receive a curated resource pack: three links our facilitators actually use, two books they would recommend if pressed, and one honest assessment of the gaps in their own knowledge of Competitive Programming and how they are addressing them. We include the last one because we think intellectual honesty about what you do not know is as valuable as knowledge itself, and we want to model that for students.

This is AI & ML Club's commitment: if you attend and feel it was not worth your time, tell us directly. We will listen and we will fix it for next time. That is how we have gotten better every semester.

title: Career Fair: Blockchain
description:
We have structured this event around a principle that Cultural Committee cares about deeply: learning by producing, not learning by consuming. Every segment of this session on Blockchain includes a moment where you must make something — a diagram, a line of code, a decision, a prediction. These are not graded. They will not be collected. They are for you, because the act of producing forces your brain to process information in a way that passive watching simply does not.

Welcome to one of the most genuinely useful events Cultural Committee has run this academic year. We know that phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let us be specific about what we mean. This session on Blockchain was designed in response to direct feedback from students who sat placement interviews, bombed questions they had never been exposed to, and came back asking us to do something about it. We listened. What you will see today is the result of six weeks of curriculum design, two rounds of feedback from working engineers, and one very honest conversation about what actually matters.

A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with Blockchain professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. But if you are hoping for a deep technical dive at the cutting edge of the field, this is not that event. We are going for breadth and confidence-building, not depth. The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

The speakers for this event have been chosen for one reason above all others: they can explain things clearly. It sounds obvious, but it is surprisingly rare. We have had sessions in the past where technically brilliant people presented information in a way that left the room more confused than when they arrived. We learnt from that. The facilitators you will hear from today have been tested in smaller settings first, given feedback, and iterated. What you are getting is a refined version, not a first draft.

The venue has been chosen specifically for its layout. We needed a room where the facilitator could move around freely, where breakout discussions could happen without disrupting the main session, and where the acoustics would not turn every explanation into an echo. We did a walkthrough last week. The space works. If you have attended events at other venues and found them frustrating for these reasons, this one should be different.

This is Cultural Committee's commitment: if you attend and feel it was not worth your time, tell us directly. We will listen and we will fix it for next time. That is how we have gotten better every semester.

title: React & Next.js Showcase
description: One thing that consistently surprises attendees at Placement Cell events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on React & Next.js — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. They are a core part of what we are trying to create. The idea for this event on React & Next.js came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews. The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for React & Next.js — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from. Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where React & Next.js was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with React & Next.js. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together. We will see you there. Bring your laptop, bring your questions, and bring someone who needs this as much as you do. Food & drinks provided. Allergies? Email us at <events@rvce.edu.in>.

title: Data Structures Sprint
description:
The idea for this event on Data Structures came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from Data Structures that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

One thing that consistently surprises attendees at Music Society events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on Data Structures — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. They are a core part of what we are trying to create.

The speakers for this event have been chosen for one reason above all others: they can explain things clearly. It sounds obvious, but it is surprisingly rare. We have had sessions in the past where technically brilliant people presented information in a way that left the room more confused than when they arrived. We learnt from that. The facilitators you will hear from today have been tested in smaller settings first, given feedback, and iterated. What you are getting is a refined version, not a first draft.

The venue has been chosen specifically for its layout. We needed a room where the facilitator could move around freely, where breakout discussions could happen without disrupting the main session, and where the acoustics would not turn every explanation into an echo. We did a walkthrough last week. The space works. If you have attended events at other venues and found them frustrating for these reasons, this one should be different.

This is Music Society's commitment: if you attend and feel it was not worth your time, tell us directly. We will listen and we will fix it for next time. That is how we have gotten better every semester.

title: Python for Beginners 101: Beginner's Guide
description:
Most events on Python for Beginners are designed for people who already have a foundation and just want to go deeper. This one is different. AI & ML Club built this session specifically for the student who has heard the term a hundred times, nodded along in class, and quietly panicked when asked to actually do something with it. You are the target audience. There is no shame in being here at the beginning — there is only the question of what you choose to do about it. This is your practical starting point.

A few things we want to be transparent about. The facilitators running this session are not perfect. They will make mistakes in live demonstrations. When that happens, we will debug together, which is arguably the most educational part of any session. AI & ML Club believes in showing real work, not curated performances. If that sounds like a good use of your Saturday afternoon, we think you will find this event genuinely worthwhile.

We have structured this event around a principle that AI & ML Club cares about deeply: learning by producing, not learning by consuming. Every segment of this session on Python for Beginners includes a moment where you must make something — a diagram, a line of code, a decision, a prediction. These are not graded. They will not be collected. They are for you, because the act of producing forces your brain to process information in a way that passive watching simply does not.

The speakers for this event have been chosen for one reason above all others: they can explain things clearly. It sounds obvious, but it is surprisingly rare. We have had sessions in the past where technically brilliant people presented information in a way that left the room more confused than when they arrived. We learnt from that. The facilitators you will hear from today have been tested in smaller settings first, given feedback, and iterated. What you are getting is a refined version, not a first draft.

The venue has been chosen specifically for its layout. We needed a room where the facilitator could move around freely, where breakout discussions could happen without disrupting the main session, and where the acoustics would not turn every explanation into an echo. We did a walkthrough last week. The space works. If you have attended events at other venues and found them frustrating for these reasons, this one should be different.

If you have read this far and you are still not registered, we genuinely want to know what is stopping you. DM us on Instagram.

title: Open Mic: Sustainable Tech

So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. title: Seminar on Public Speaking
description:
Welcome to one of the most genuinely useful events Eco Warriors has run this academic year. We know that phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let us be specific about what we mean. This session on Public Speaking was designed in response to direct feedback from students who sat placement interviews, bombed questions they had never been exposed to, and came back asking us to do something about it. We listened. What you will see today is the result of six weeks of curriculum design, two rounds of feedback from working engineers, and one very honest conversation about what actually matters.

A few things we want to be transparent about. The facilitators running this session are not perfect. They will make mistakes in live demonstrations. When that happens, we will debug together, which is arguably the most educational part of any session. Eco Warriors believes in showing real work, not curated performances. If that sounds like a good use of your Saturday afternoon, we think you will find this event genuinely worthwhile.

We have structured this event around a principle that Eco Warriors cares about deeply: learning by producing, not learning by consuming. Every segment of this session on Public Speaking includes a moment where you must make something — a diagram, a line of code, a decision, a prediction. These are not graded. They will not be collected. They are for you, because the act of producing forces your brain to process information in a way that passive watching simply does not.

The speakers for this event have been chosen for one reason above all others: they can explain things clearly. It sounds obvious, but it is surprisingly rare. We have had sessions in the past where technically brilliant people presented information in a way that left the room more confused than when they arrived. We learnt from that. The facilitators you will hear from today have been tested in smaller settings first, given feedback, and iterated. What you are getting is a refined version, not a first draft.

Certificates of participation will be issued to everyone who attends. We know that is a secondary concern for most people in this room, and we are glad for that. But for those who need it — for internship applications, for placement interviews, for anxious parents — it exists and it will arrive in your inbox within 48 hours of the event's close. Please register with your college email address to ensure delivery.

Show up. Work hard. Leave better. That is all we ask.

title: Career Fair: AR/VR Development
description:
A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with AR/VR Development professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. But if you are hoping for a deep technical dive at the cutting edge of the field, this is not that event. We are going for breadth and confidence-building, not depth. The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

We have structured this event around a principle that Design Guild cares about deeply: learning by producing, not learning by consuming. Every segment of this session on AR/VR Development includes a moment where you must make something — a diagram, a line of code, a decision, a prediction. These are not graded. They will not be collected. They are for you, because the act of producing forces your brain to process information in a way that passive watching simply does not.

Most events on AR/VR Development are designed for people who already have a foundation and just want to go deeper. This one is different. Design Guild built this session specifically for the student who has heard the term a hundred times, nodded along in class, and quietly panicked when asked to actually do something with it. You are the target audience. There is no shame in being here at the beginning — there is only the question of what you choose to do about it. This is your practical starting point.

We considered bringing in an external speaker for this one and decided against it. The best person to talk to RVCE students about navigating AR/VR Development in the current environment is someone who was an RVCE student recently enough to remember what it felt like — and senior enough to have perspective on it. That is what we have. Someone who has been where you are, done what you are trying to do, and is willing to be honest about how they actually got there.

After the event, all registered attendees will receive a curated resource pack: three links our facilitators actually use, two books they would recommend if pressed, and one honest assessment of the gaps in their own knowledge of AR/VR Development and how they are addressing them. We include the last one because we think intellectual honesty about what you do not know is as valuable as knowledge itself, and we want to model that for students.

The event is free. The knowledge is permanent. The registration takes thirty seconds. There is no reason not to.

title: Research Methodology Bootcamp
description:
We want to be upfront about what this event is not. It is not a placement coaching session. It is not a certificate farm. It is not a box to tick on your co-curricular activity sheet. It is a room full of people who are genuinely curious about Research Methodology, facilitated by people who have invested real time in understanding it, with the goal of leaving everyone slightly less confused than they arrived. If that sounds like a good way to spend a few hours, the door is open.

Here is what the session actually looks like. We open with a fifteen-minute orientation that covers the landscape of Research Methodology — where it sits relative to everything else you have learned, why it matters now more than it did five years ago, and what a working professional actually does with it on a Monday morning. This part is deliberately fast. We do not want to spend half the session on theory that you could have absorbed from a Wikipedia article. We want to get to the part where you do things.

Welcome to one of the most genuinely useful events Coding Club RVCE has run this academic year. We know that phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let us be specific about what we mean. This session on Research Methodology was designed in response to direct feedback from students who sat placement interviews, bombed questions they had never been exposed to, and came back asking us to do something about it. We listened. What you will see today is the result of six weeks of curriculum design, two rounds of feedback from working engineers, and one very honest conversation about what actually matters.

We considered bringing in an external speaker for this one and decided against it. The best person to talk to RVCE students about navigating Research Methodology in the current environment is someone who was an RVCE student recently enough to remember what it felt like — and senior enough to have perspective on it. The venue has been chosen specifically for its layout. We needed a room where the facilitator could move around freely, where breakout discussions could happen without disrupting the main session, and where the acoustics would not turn every explanation into an echo. title: Web Dev Workshop: Robotics & Automation
description:
There is a version of this event that would have been easy to run — a polished slide deck, a speaker talking at you for ninety minutes, a group photo at the end. We chose not to do that version. Instead, the Quizzing Club spent the last month building a session on Robotics & Automation that puts you in the driver's seat from the first minute. The facilitators are here as guides, not lecturers. The agenda is a suggestion, not a script. And the only metric we care about at the end is whether you leave more capable than when you arrived.

A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with Robotics & Automation professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. But if you are hoping for a deep technical dive at the cutting edge of the field, this is not that event. We are going for breadth and confidence-building, not depth. The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for Robotics & Automation — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

Food and drinks will be available throughout. We mention this not to bribe you into attending — the content should do that — but because we have noticed that sessions run better when people are not hungry. Please eat something before you arrive as well. A three-hour session on Robotics & Automation on an empty stomach is not the optimal learning environment, and we speak from experience.

We will see you there. Bring your laptop, bring your questions, and bring someone who needs this as much as you do.

title: Open Source Contribution Sprint
description:
A few things we want to be transparent about. The facilitators running this session are not perfect. They will make mistakes in live demonstrations. When that happens, we will debug together, which is arguably the most educational part of any session. AI & ML Club believes in showing real work, not curated performances. If that sounds like a good use of your Saturday afternoon, we think you will find this event genuinely worthwhile.

The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from Open Source Contribution that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

There is a version of this event that would have been easy to run — a polished slide deck, a speaker talking at you for ninety minutes, a group photo at the end. We chose not to do that version. Instead, the AI & ML Club spent the last month building a session on Open Source Contribution that puts you in the driver's seat from the first minute. The facilitators are here as guides, not lecturers. The agenda is a suggestion, not a script. And the only metric we care about at the end is whether you leave more capable than when you arrived.

The venue has been chosen specifically for its layout. We needed a room where the facilitator could move around freely, where breakout discussions could happen without disrupting the main session, and where the acoustics would not turn every explanation into an echo. We did a walkthrough last week. The space works. If you have attended events at other venues and found them frustrating for these reasons, this one should be different.

Show up. Work hard. Leave better. That is all we ask.

title: Career Fair: Photography Basics
description:
Welcome to one of the most genuinely useful events Quizzing Club has run this academic year. We know that phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let us be specific about what we mean. This session on Photography Basics was designed in response to direct feedback from students who sat placement interviews, bombed questions they had never been exposed to, and came back asking us to do something about it. We listened. What you will see today is the result of six weeks of curriculum design, two rounds of feedback from working engineers, and one very honest conversation about what actually matters.

We want to be upfront about what this event is not. It is not a placement coaching session. It is not a certificate farm. It is not a box to tick on your co-curricular activity sheet. It is a room full of people who are genuinely curious about Photography Basics, facilitated by people who have invested real time in understanding it, with the goal of leaving everyone slightly less confused than they arrived. If that sounds like a good way to spend a few hours, the door is open.

Here is what the session actually looks like. We open with a fifteen-minute orientation that covers the landscape of Photography Basics — where it sits relative to everything else you have learned, why it matters now more than it did five years ago, and what a working professional actually does with it on a Monday morning. This part is deliberately fast. We do not want to spend half the session on theory that you could have absorbed from a Wikipedia article. We want to get to the part where you do things.

Registration is open now. Space is limited. If you are on the fence, the fence is the wrong place to be.

title: Blockchain 101: Beginner's Guide
description:
We have structured this event around a principle that AI & ML Club cares about deeply: learning by producing, not learning by consuming. Every segment of this session on Blockchain includes a moment where you must make something — a diagram, a line of code, a decision, a prediction. These are not graded. They will not be collected. They are for you, because the act of producing forces your brain to process information in a way that passive watching simply does not.

The idea for this event on Blockchain came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

A few things we want to be transparent about. The facilitators running this session are not perfect. They will make mistakes in live demonstrations. When that happens, we will debug together, which is arguably the most educational part of any session. AI & ML Club believes in showing real work, not curated performances. If that sounds like a good use of your Saturday afternoon, we think you will find this event genuinely worthwhile.

The person leading today's session on Blockchain was not our first choice — they were our third. Our first two choices were excellent but unavailable on this date. Our third choice turned out to be better than either of the first two, which is a useful reminder that the best facilitators are not always the most obvious ones. They bring a perspective on Blockchain that we had not fully anticipated when we reached out, and we think it makes the session richer for it.

This is AI & ML Club's commitment: if you attend and feel it was not worth your time, tell us directly. We will listen and we will fix it for next time. That is how we have gotten better every semester.

title: UI/UX Design Bootcamp
description:
Welcome to one of the most genuinely useful events Robotics Club has run this academic year. We know that phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let us be specific about what we mean. This session on UI/UX Design was designed in response to direct feedback from students who sat placement interviews, bombed questions they had never been exposed to, and came back asking us to do something about it. We listened. What you will see today is the result of six weeks of curriculum design, two rounds of feedback from working engineers, and one very honest conversation about what actually matters.

We want to be upfront about what this event is not. It is not a placement coaching session. It is not a certificate farm. It is not a box to tick on your co-curricular activity sheet. It is a room full of people who are genuinely curious about UI/UX Design, facilitated by people who have invested real time in understanding it, with the goal of leaving everyone slightly less confused than they arrived. If that sounds like a good way to spend a few hours, the door is open.

The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for UI/UX Design — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where UI/UX Design was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with UI/UX Design. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together.

Food and drinks will be available throughout. We mention this not to bribe you into attending — the content should do that — but because we have noticed that sessions run better when people are not hungry. Please eat something before you arrive as well. A three-hour session on UI/UX Design on an empty stomach is not the optimal learning environment, and we speak from experience.

Show up. Work hard. Leave better. That is all we ask.

title: Cloud Computing Bootcamp
description:
Welcome to one of the most genuinely useful events Drama Club has run this academic year. We know that phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let us be specific about what we mean. This session on Cloud Computing was designed in response to direct feedback from students who sat placement interviews, bombed questions they had never been exposed to, and came back asking us to do something about it. We listened. What you will see today is the result of six weeks of curriculum design, two rounds of feedback from working engineers, and one very honest conversation about what actually matters.

A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with Cloud Computing professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. But if you are hoping for a deep technical dive at the cutting edge of the field, this is not that event. We are going for breadth and confidence-building, not depth. The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from Cloud Computing that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where Cloud Computing was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with Cloud Computing. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together.

After the event, all registered attendees will receive a curated resource pack: three links our facilitators actually use, two books they would recommend if pressed, and one honest assessment of the gaps in their own knowledge of Cloud Computing and how they are addressing them. We include the last one because we think intellectual honesty about what you do not know is as valuable as knowledge itself, and we want to model that for students.

We will see you there. Bring your laptop, bring your questions, and bring someone who needs this as much as you do.

title: System Design Hackathon
description:
The idea for this event on System Design came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

We want to be upfront about what this event is not. It is not a placement coaching session. It is not a certificate farm. It is not a box to tick on your co-curricular activity sheet. It is a room full of people who are genuinely curious about System Design, facilitated by people who have invested real time in understanding it, with the goal of leaving everyone slightly less confused than they arrived. If that sounds like a good way to spend a few hours, the door is open.

The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from System Design that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

Registration is open now. Space is limited. If you are on the fence, the fence is the wrong place to be.

title: Web Dev Workshop: REST APIs
description:
One thing that consistently surprises attendees at Cybersecurity Club events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on REST APIs — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. They are a core part of what we are trying to create.

The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for REST APIs — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

The idea for this event on REST APIs came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

We considered bringing in an external speaker for this one and decided against it. The best person to talk to RVCE students about navigating REST APIs in the current environment is someone who was an RVCE student recently enough to remember what it felt like — and senior enough to have perspective on it. That is what we have. Someone who has been where you are, done what you are trying to do, and is willing to be honest about how they actually got there.

If you have read this far and you are still not registered, we genuinely want to know what is stopping you. DM us on Instagram.

title: REST APIs — Guest Lecture
description:
The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from REST APIs that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

Welcome to one of the most genuinely useful events AI & ML Club has run this academic year. We know that phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let us be specific about what we mean. This session on REST APIs was designed in response to direct feedback from students who sat placement interviews, bombed questions they had never been exposed to, and came back asking us to do something about it. We listened. What you will see today is the result of six weeks of curriculum design, two rounds of feedback from working engineers, and one very honest conversation about what actually matters.

A few things we want to be transparent about. The facilitators running this session are not perfect. They will make mistakes in live demonstrations. When that happens, we will debug together, which is arguably the most educational part of any session. AI & ML Club believes in showing real work, not curated performances. If that sounds like a good use of your Saturday afternoon, we think you will find this event genuinely worthwhile.

After the event, all registered attendees will receive a curated resource pack: three links our facilitators actually use, two books they would recommend if pressed, and one honest assessment of the gaps in their own knowledge of REST APIs and how they are addressing them. We include the last one because we think intellectual honesty about what you do not know is as valuable as knowledge itself, and we want to model that for students.

This is AI & ML Club's commitment: if you attend and feel it was not worth your time, tell us directly. We will listen and we will fix it for next time. That is how we have gotten better every semester.

title: Networking Night: Sustainable Tech
description:
The idea for this event on Sustainable Tech came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

One thing that consistently surprises attendees at Quizzing Club events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on Sustainable Tech — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. Here is what the session actually looks like. We open with a fifteen-minute orientation that covers the landscape of Sustainable Tech — where it sits relative to everything else you have learned, why it matters now more than it did five years ago, and what a working professional actually does with it on a Monday morning. This part is deliberately fast. We do not want to spend half the session on theory that you could have absorbed from a Wikipedia article. We want to get to the part where you do things.

Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where Sustainable Tech was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with Sustainable Tech. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together.

title: Industry Talk: Embedded Systems
description: Welcome to one of the most genuinely useful events Cybersecurity Club has run this academic year. We know that phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let us be specific about what we mean. This session on Embedded Systems was designed in response to direct feedback from students who sat placement interviews, bombed questions they had never been exposed to, and came back asking us to do something about it. We listened. What you will see today is the result of six weeks of curriculum design, two rounds of feedback from working engineers, and one very honest conversation about what actually matters. We want to be upfront about what this event is not. It is not a placement coaching session. It is not a certificate farm. It is not a box to tick on your co-curricular activity sheet. It is a room full of people who are genuinely curious about Embedded Systems, facilitated by people who have invested real time in understanding it, with the goal of leaving everyone slightly less confused than they arrived. If that sounds like a good way to spend a few hours, the door is open. We have structured this event around a principle that Cybersecurity Club cares about deeply: learning by producing, not learning by consuming. Every segment of this session on Embedded Systems includes a moment where you must make something — a diagram, a line of code, a decision, a prediction. These are not graded. They will not be collected. They are for you, because the act of producing forces your brain to process information in a way that passive watching simply does not. After the event, all registered attendees will receive a curated resource pack: three links our facilitators actually use, two books they would recommend if pressed, and one honest assessment of the gaps in their own knowledge of Embedded Systems and how they are addressing them. We include the last one because we think intellectual honesty about what you do not know is as valuable as knowledge itself, and we want to model that for students. This is Cybersecurity Club's commitment: if you attend and feel it was not worth your time, tell us directly. We will listen and we will fix it for next time. That is how we have gotten better every semester. Food & drinks provided. Allergies? Email us at <events@rvce.edu.in>.

title: Hands-on REST APIs Session
description:
Welcome to one of the most genuinely useful events Cultural Committee has run this academic year. We know that phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let us be specific about what we mean. We listened. What you will see today is the result of six weeks of curriculum design, two rounds of feedback from working engineers, and one very honest conversation about what actually matters.

A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with REST APIs professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for REST APIs — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. The speakers for this event have been chosen for one reason above all others: they can explain things clearly. It sounds obvious, but it is surprisingly rare. We have had sessions in the past where technically brilliant people presented information in a way that left the room more confused than when they arrived. We learnt from that. The facilitators you will hear from today have been tested in smaller settings first, given feedback, and iterated. What you are getting is a refined version, not a first draft.

The venue has been chosen specifically for its layout. We needed a room where the facilitator could move around freely, where breakout discussions could happen without disrupting the main session, and where the acoustics would not turn every explanation into an echo. We did a walkthrough last week. The space works. If you have attended events at other venues and found them frustrating for these reasons, this one should be different.

If you have read this far and you are still not registered, we genuinely want to know what is stopping you. DM us on Instagram.

title: Networking Night: Blockchain
description:
Welcome to one of the most genuinely useful events Finance Club has run this academic year. We know that phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let us be specific about what we mean. This session on Blockchain was designed in response to direct feedback from students who sat placement interviews, bombed questions they had never been exposed to, and came back asking us to do something about it. We listened. What you will see today is the result of six weeks of curriculum design, two rounds of feedback from working engineers, and one very honest conversation about what actually matters.

One thing that consistently surprises attendees at Finance Club events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on Blockchain — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. They are a core part of what we are trying to create.

Here is what the session actually looks like. We open with a fifteen-minute orientation that covers the landscape of Blockchain — where it sits relative to everything else you have learned, why it matters now more than it did five years ago, and what a working professional actually does with it on a Monday morning. This part is deliberately fast. We do not want to spend half the session on theory that you could have absorbed from a Wikipedia article. We want to get to the part where you do things.

We considered bringing in an external speaker for this one and decided against it. The best person to talk to RVCE students about navigating Blockchain in the current environment is someone who was an RVCE student recently enough to remember what it felt like — and senior enough to have perspective on it. That is what we have. Someone who has been where you are, done what you are trying to do, and is willing to be honest about how they actually got there.

After the event, all registered attendees will receive a curated resource pack: three links our facilitators actually use, two books they would recommend if pressed, and one honest assessment of the gaps in their own knowledge of Blockchain and how they are addressing them. We include the last one because we think intellectual honesty about what you do not know is as valuable as knowledge itself, and we want to model that for students.

The event is free. The knowledge is permanent. The registration takes thirty seconds. There is no reason not to.

title: Hands-on React & Next.js Session
description:
The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from React & Next.js that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with React & Next.js professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. But if you are hoping for a deep technical dive at the cutting edge of the field, this is not that event. We are going for breadth and confidence-building, not depth. The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

Most events on React & Next.js are designed for people who already have a foundation and just want to go deeper. This one is different. Coding Club RVCE built this session specifically for the student who has heard the term a hundred times, nodded along in class, and quietly panicked when asked to actually do something with it. You are the target audience. There is no shame in being here at the beginning — there is only the question of what you choose to do about it. This is your practical starting point.

Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where React & Next.js was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with React & Next.js. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together.

Food and drinks will be available throughout. We mention this not to bribe you into attending — the content should do that — but because we have noticed that sessions run better when people are not hungry. Please eat something before you arrive as well. A three-hour session on React & Next.js on an empty stomach is not the optimal learning environment, and we speak from experience.

If you have read this far and you are still not registered, we genuinely want to know what is stopping you. DM us on Instagram.

title: REST APIs Bootcamp
description:
A few things we want to be transparent about. The facilitators running this session are not perfect. They will make mistakes in live demonstrations. When that happens, we will debug together, which is arguably the most educational part of any session. Astronomy Club believes in showing real work, not curated performances. If that sounds like a good use of your Saturday afternoon, we think you will find this event genuinely worthwhile.

Welcome to one of the most genuinely useful events Astronomy Club has run this academic year. We know that phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let us be specific about what we mean. This session on REST APIs was designed in response to direct feedback from students who sat placement interviews, bombed questions they had never been exposed to, and came back asking us to do something about it. We listened. What you will see today is the result of six weeks of curriculum design, two rounds of feedback from working engineers, and one very honest conversation about what actually matters.

The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for REST APIs — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

Show up. Work hard. Leave better. That is all we ask.

title: Open Mic: Game Development
description:
There is a version of this event that would have been easy to run — a polished slide deck, a speaker talking at you for ninety minutes, a group photo at the end. We chose not to do that version. Instead, the Literary Club spent the last month building a session on Game Development that puts you in the driver's seat from the first minute. The facilitators are here as guides, not lecturers. The agenda is a suggestion, not a script. And the only metric we care about at the end is whether you leave more capable than when you arrived.

The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for Game Development — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

One thing that consistently surprises attendees at Literary Club events is how much of the value comes from the people in the room rather than from the facilitators. We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on Game Development — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. They are a core part of what we are trying to create.

The person leading today's session on Game Development was not our first choice — they were our third. Our first two choices were excellent but unavailable on this date. Our third choice turned out to be better than either of the first two, which is a useful reminder that the best facilitators are not always the most obvious ones. They bring a perspective on Game Development that we had not fully anticipated when we reached out, and we think it makes the session richer for it.

If you have read this far and you are still not registered, we genuinely want to know what is stopping you. DM us on Instagram.

description:

title: Robotics & Automation — Guest Lecture
description:

The idea for this event on Robotics & Automation came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with Robotics & Automation professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. But if you are hoping for a deep technical dive at the cutting edge of the field, this is not that event. We are going for breadth and confidence-building, not depth. The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

We will see you there. Bring your laptop, bring your questions, and bring someone who needs this as much as you do.

title: Open Mic: Finance 101
description:
Most events on Finance 101 are designed for people who already have a foundation and just want to go deeper. This one is different. Cybersecurity Club built this session specifically for the student who has heard the term a hundred times, nodded along in class, and quietly panicked when asked to actually do something with it. You are the target audience. There is no shame in being here at the beginning — there is only the question of what you choose to do about it. This is your practical starting point.

The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from Finance 101 that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

When that happens, we will debug together, which is arguably the most educational part of any session. Cybersecurity Club believes in showing real work, not curated performances. If that sounds like a good use of your Saturday afternoon, we think you will find this event genuinely worthwhile.

Food and drinks will be available throughout. We mention this not to bribe you into attending — the content should do that — but because we have noticed that sessions run better when people are not hungry. Please eat something before you arrive as well. A three-hour session on Finance 101 on an empty stomach is not the optimal learning environment, and we speak from experience.

title: Cloud Computing Bootcamp
description:

We are deliberately bringing together students from across years and branches for this session on Cloud Computing — the conversations that happen at the break, the connections that get made on the way out, the WhatsApp groups that form spontaneously — these are not a side effect of the event. The idea for this event on AR/VR Development came from a conversation between three final-year students in our club who were preparing for placement season. They realised that despite four years of engineering education, they could not confidently answer basic interview questions on this topic. That felt wrong. So they built a session to fix it — for themselves first, and then for everyone else. What you are walking into today is the third iteration of that original conversation, refined by real feedback from real students who have been through real interviews.

We have structured this event around a principle that Finance Club cares about deeply: learning by producing, not learning by consuming. Every segment of this session on AR/VR Development includes a moment where you must make something — a diagram, a line of code, a decision, a prediction. These are not graded. They will not be collected. They are for you, because the act of producing forces your brain to process information in a way that passive watching simply does not.

A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with AR/VR Development professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. But if you are hoping for a deep technical dive at the cutting edge of the field, this is not that event. We are going for breadth and confidence-building, not depth. The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where AR/VR Development was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with AR/VR Development. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together.

Show up. Work hard. Leave better. That is all we ask.
