title: Open Mic: Game Development
description:
Welcome to one of the most genuinely useful events Open Source Club has run this academic year. We know that phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let us be specific about what we mean. This session on Game Development was designed in response to direct feedback from students who sat placement interviews, bombed questions they had never been exposed to, and came back asking us to do something about it. We listened. What you will see today is the result of six weeks of curriculum design, two rounds of feedback from working engineers, and one very honest conversation about what actually matters.

We want to be upfront about what this event is not. It is not a placement coaching session. It is not a certificate farm. It is not a box to tick on your co-curricular activity sheet. It is a room full of people who are genuinely curious about Game Development, facilitated by people who have invested real time in understanding it, with the goal of leaving everyone slightly less confused than they arrived. If that sounds like a good way to spend a few hours, the door is open.

The structure is deliberately non-linear. We start with a problem — something real, something broken, something that needs fixing. Then we introduce the concept from Game Development that solves it. This is the opposite of how most courses teach the subject, and the research on retention strongly suggests it is also more effective. You remember a concept much better when you have already felt the pain of not having it than when you are introduced to it in the abstract and told it will be useful someday.

Our speakers come from three different backgrounds: one is currently in their final year at RVCE and recently completed an internship where Game Development was central to their work; one graduated two years ago and now works at a product company in Bangalore; and one is a postgraduate student whose research intersects directly with Game Development. Three perspectives, three contexts, one coherent session. We spent significant time aligning their content to make sure the session flows rather than feeling like three separate talks stapled together.

Food and drinks will be available throughout. We mention this not to bribe you into attending — the content should do that — but because we have noticed that sessions run better when people are not hungry. Please eat something before you arrive as well. A three-hour session on Game Development on an empty stomach is not the optimal learning environment, and we speak from experience.

Registration is open now. Space is limited. If you are on the fence, the fence is the wrong place to be.

This session on UI/UX Design was designed in response to direct feedback from students who sat placement interviews, bombed questions they had never been exposed to, and came back asking us to do something about it. We listened. What you will see today is the result of six weeks of curriculum design, two rounds of feedback from working engineers, and one very honest conversation about what actually matters.

A word on who this event is for, because we want to be honest about it. If you already work deeply with UI/UX Design professionally, this session will probably feel slow in places. You are welcome to come, contribute, and help others — that peer teaching dynamic is something we actively encourage. But if you are hoping for a deep technical dive at the cutting edge of the field, this is not that event. We are going for breadth and confidence-building, not depth. The deep dive version is on our roadmap for next semester.

The session is divided into three working blocks, each forty minutes long, with a ten-minute break between each. In the first block, we lay the conceptual groundwork for UI/UX Design — quickly, clearly, without unnecessary jargon. In the second block, we work through three progressively harder problems together, live, with full narration of the thinking process. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.

We considered bringing in an external speaker for this one and decided against it. The best person to talk to RVCE students about navigating UI/UX Design in the current environment is someone who was an RVCE student recently enough to remember what it felt like — and senior enough to have perspective on it. That is what we have. Someone who has been where you are, done what you are trying to do, and is willing to be honest about how they actually got there.

Certificates of participation will be issued to everyone who attends. We know that is a secondary concern for most people in this room, and we are glad for that. But for those who need it — for internship applications, for placement interviews, for anxious parents — it exists and it will arrive in your inbox within 48 hours of the event's close. Please register with your college email address to ensure delivery.

Seats will run out before the deadline does. Register now.

Food and drinks will be available throughout. In the third block, you work independently on a problem while the facilitators circulate and give one-on-one feedback. This is the block most attendees say they learn the most from.
